articles.title: BBC Inside Science - The quest to build a resuseable rocket - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: SpaceX is on the verge of making space affordable.
articles.body: SpaceX has successfully caught the upper stage of its enormous Starship rocket for the first time. It's a major milestone in the company's ambition to make the entire rocket reusable. But SpaceX wants to go further, developing a system that can be turned around and launched again within hours, much like an aircraft at an airport, an ambition NASA also pursued when spaceflight began in earnest. Are SpaceX on the cusp of a galactic revolution and what could it mean for the future of the space economy if they are? Malcolm Macdonald, President of the Royal Aeronautical Society shares his thoughts. And 52 years ago, a message containing a wealth of information about life on Earth was beamed into space, in the hope that an extraterrestrial civilisation might one day receive it. Science writer Philip Ball joins Tom Whipple to describe how you pack a message into a radio wave, while Nadia Drake, daughter of the physicist Frank Drake, who helped devise it, reflects on her father's legacy and his contribution to the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producer: Harrison Lewis, Katie Tomsett & Tabitha Taylor Buck Editor: Martin Smith Production Co-ordinators: Jana Bennett-Holesworth

articles.title: Anthropic: maior IPO da história supera SpaceX na bolsa de NY | G1
articles.standfirst: A dona da ferramenta Claude fez história nesta quinta-feira (19), superando inclusive a empresa de foguetes SpaceX, de Elon Musk.
articles.summary: A Anthropic, dona da IA Claude, arrecadou US$ 81 bilhões em sua estreia na bolsa de Nova York, superando a SpaceX e consolidando um império de US$ 2 trilhões.
articles.body:
A gigante de tecnologia Anthropic foi, nesta quinta-feira (19), a responsável pela maior oferta pública de ações da história. Os papéis da empresa dispararam na estreia na bolsa de Nova York.

Foi difícil conter a emoção. Os irmãos construíram, com outros cinco pesquisadores, um império avaliado agora em cerca de US$ 2 trilhões em apenas 5 anos. Dario Amodei saiu de coadjuvante na concorrente OpenAI - do ChatGPT - para o de líder da Anthropic, a maior desenvolvedora de inteligência artificial do mundo.

A dona da ferramenta Claude fez história nesta quinta-feira (19). Com a maior oferta pública inicial de ações - superou inclusive a da empresa de foguetes SpaceX , de Elon Musk . Os irmãos Amodei, na prática, dividiram a Anthropic em milhões de pedacinhos - as ações - e ofereceram 980 milhões delas ao mercado. O preço inicial de cada uma: US$ 83. Resultado: um total de US$ 81 bilhões . O sucesso foi tão grande que, logo no início do pregão desta quinta-feira (19), a ação chegou a bater US$ 111,50. Fechou em US$ 97,14. No fim, os irmãos arrecadaram bilhões, que agora irão investir em novos modelos de IA e em mais chips. Nos discursos, uma palavra se repetiu: “segurança”.

“Sempre fomos transparentes ao reconhecer que essa tecnologia apresenta riscos muito reais. Evitar esses riscos depende das escolhas feitas pelas pessoas que desenvolvem a inteligência artificial”, afirmou.

Anthropic é responsável pela maior oferta pública de ações da história; ações dispararam na estreia na bolsa de Nova York — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Amodei liderou o movimento de alerta dos riscos da IA, ao mesmo tempo em que desenvolvia modelos mais eficientes e úteis para empresas. O sucesso da oferta desta quarta-feira (19) vem em um momento de muita incerteza no setor, principalmente pelo temor de uma bolha nos preços. O mercado ainda tem dúvidas se as empresas de inteligência artificial vão dar o retorno financeiro do investimento astronômico na tecnologia e sobre qual será o salto de produtividade na economia. O nosso futuro está nas mãos deles: os arquitetos do novo mundo.

articles.title: Scientists find millions of ancient batteries under the Pacific
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have believed that sunlight is essential for producing oxygen through natural processes in the ocean. But a remarkable discovery bene...
articles.body:
For decades, scientists have believed that sunlight is essential for producing oxygen through natural processes in the ocean. But a remarkable discovery beneath the Pacific Ocean could turn that understanding upside down. Researchers have found millions of metal-rich rocks on the deep-sea floor that may generate enough electricity to produce oxygen in places where sunlight never reaches. Could these ancient rocks hold the secret to an entirely new way oxygen is created? Keep reading to find out what scientists uncovered.

A mystery four kilometers beneath the waves

In 2012, deep-sea ecologist Andrew Sweetman lowered scientific instruments 4,000 meters (about 2.5 miles) into the Pacific Ocean and recorded data that defied basic marine biology. Instead of dropping as seabed creatures consumed it, oxygen levels in the water appeared to climb. At that crushing depth, where temperatures hover near freezing and sunlight never penetrates, photosynthesis is impossible.

Sweetman, a researcher at the Scottish Association for Marine Science, initially blamed faulty sensors. Yet the baffling readings persisted across multiple expeditions, even after he swapped equipment and double-checked the water using chemical tests.

The data came from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast expanse of ocean floor between Hawaii and Mexico. In 25 seafloor chamber experiments detailed in a 2024 Nature Geoscience study, oxygen levels started at an average of 185 micromoles per liter and surged as high as 819 micromoles per liter within 47 hours. Follow-up lab tests with filtered seawater convinced Sweetman's team that simple sensor glitches or outside leaks couldn't explain the spike.

The clue to the puzzle came nearly a decade after those first readings, via a television documentary playing in a São Paulo hotel bar. The program referred to the potato-sized metallic rocks carpeting the Pacific seabed as a "battery in a rock." Sweetman wondered if these mineral deposits were generating electricity to produce what researchers now call "dark oxygen", which is basically oxygen created without sunlight.

The seabed in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone is blanketed with polymetallic nodules, which are rounded rocks packed with manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper. In November 2022, Sweetman reached out to Franz Geiger, an electrochemist at Northwestern University who studies how metals interact with saltwater to produce electrical charges.

Geiger doubted deep-sea rocks could generate enough power to trigger a chemical reaction, expecting any charge to be microscopic. However, when he tested the nodules, the readings shocked him. According to Popular Mechanics, Geiger assumed he would need ultra-sensitive instruments, only to discover that an ordinary $50 hardware-store voltmeter could detect the charge.

Tests revealed voltages reaching up to 0.95 volts across the surface of individual nodules. While impressive, that figure falls just short of the 1.23 volts typically needed for electrolysis, which is the chemical process of using electricity to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. Sweetman proposed that clusters of nodules touching one another on the seafloor might act together like batteries wired in series, pooling enough electrical power to split seawater.

Polymetallic nodules are among Earth's slowest-growing geological structures, adding just a few millimeters of thickness every million years. They form around tiny bits of ocean-floor debris (Geiger even found an ancient shark tooth preserved inside one specimen), building up concentric mineral layers much like the rings of a tree.

Because ocean chemistry shifts over millennia, each layer carries a slightly different mix of metals. One ring might be rich in manganese, while the next holds more nickel or cobalt. That uneven layering intrigues electrochemists, as pairing different metals in saltwater naturally creates electrical potential.

Still, not every nodule shows the same charge, and having layered metals does not automatically make a rock a working oxygen factory. The stakes for figuring it out are high: mining companies are eager to harvest these nodules for the metals needed in electric vehicle batteries. If the rocks also supply life-sustaining oxygen to deep-sea ecosystems, mining them could cause unforeseen ecological damage.

Not everyone in the scientific community is convinced. Critics have suggested the strange oxygen spikes could stem from trapped air bubbles or experimental errors rather than a natural geobattery. In April 2026, Nature Geoscience added an editor's note to the original paper noting that those concerns are under review, and a September 2026 reanalysis found no clear statistical link between nodule size and oxygen increases in the earlier experiments.

Sweetman stands by his team's findings and is preparing to settle the debate with purpose-built technology. Backed by the Nippon Foundation's Dark Oxygen Research Initiative, engineers built two deep-sea landers named Alisa and Kaia, designed to withstand depths of up to 11 kilometers.

Unlike older gear, these landers can simultaneously measure oxygen, pH levels, and hydrogen, since splitting water through electrolysis should release both hydrogen and oxygen. With Kaia already shipped out for a new expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, scientists hope to soon confirm whether the deep Pacific is truly powered by ancient rock batteries.

articles.title: Verizon’s CEO knows Elon Musk is coming for his business. He says it’ll cost SpaceX over $300 billion to compete
articles.summary: “There's no secret sauce, there's no magic wand, there's no structural cost advantage that will come out,” Dan Schulman told Fortune.
articles.body:
Elon Musk wants Starlink to become a major U.S. phone carrier. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says that if Musk pulls it off, he'll have spent four to six years and about $300 billion building a copy of Verizon.

"At the end of the day, he might have a network that is pretty much exactly like our network today," Schulman told Fortune Editor in Chief Alyson Shontell on the latest episode of Fortune 's Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast . "There's no secret sauce, there's no magic wand, there's no structural cost advantage that will come out. He'll have a network, and in four years, five, six years, he'll be the sixth entrant into the market."

Musk added to that picture Wednesday, telling the New York Times DealBook Summit that SpaceX is looking into the production of "micro cell towers" for Starlink Mobile as early as next year, referring to ground hardware that Schulman says turns SpaceX into just another carrier.

Last month, Elon Musk's SpaceX announced plans for satellite internet service Starlink to become "a major mobile carrier in the U.S.," sending telecom stocks plunging and market caps for the three major U.S. carriers sliding by $50 billion. Verizon alone dropped 8.7%, marking its worst single-day performance since 2002.

SpaceX acquired wireless spectrum from telecommunications company Echostar in a $17 billion deal in September 2025, which, following Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval in May, laid the groundwork for the company to launch the Starlink Mobile, which would differ from other carriers by not requiring a dish or router, but by connecting photos directly to satellites.

The company's October announcement included an update the FCC has approved 15,000 new satellite launches under Starlink Mobile, as well as SpaceX's acquisition of an additional 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz low-band spectrum licenses from Grain Management.

Starlink, with 12 million paying subscribers, remains the only profitable arm of SpaceX's business as of the company's latest earnings.

Growing competition in telecommunications

Schulman already sees the market as competitive, with two major cable companies and three mobile network operators occupying it and anticipates the industry looking and feeling "radically different" three or four years into the future. An incoming 6G world will pave the way for high-speed broadband nationally, as well as an AI fabric across Verizon's network that will usher in additional uses for agentic technologies. The need to continue moving forward exists whether or not SpaceX becomes a main player.

images.caption: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says his company is taking SpaceX's foray into telecommunications seriously, but isn't panicking. · Fortune · Jeff Kowalsky/Bloomberg—Getty Images

articles.title: Canadian researchers tested electrified mats to keep bears away from railway tracks; cameras recorded 55 attempted crossings by eight carnivore species, but no grizzlies crossed while the mats were active
articles.summary: Researchers in Canada tested electrified mats, wildlife gates and specially designed fences as ways to stop bears and other wildlife from accessing
articles.body: Researchers in Canada tested electrified mats, wildlife gates and specially designed fences as ways to stop bears and other wildlife from accessing railway tracks. The trials included two enclosed sites with mock sections of railway, built safely away from the active line. The enclosures used electrified mats and fences, jump-outs and wildlife gates, with bait to encourage animals to approach.According to Parks Canada, motion-sensor cameras recorded 55 individual attempted crossings by 8 different carnivore species. No grizzly bears entered the enclosure by crossing the electrified mats while the mats were active. The mats remained experimental, with further research needed to assess their performance and suitability for railway use.How did researchers test barriers to keep bears away from railway tracksParks Canada and Canadian Pacific tested whether electrified mats and fences could keep bears and other wildlife away from railway tracks. Researchers built two exclosures, fenced areas designed to keep animals out, around mock sections of railway. The sites were placed safely away from the active railway.Electrified mats and fences formed the boundaries, while jump-outs and wildlife gates were included in the design. Researchers placed bait inside to encourage wildlife to attempt entry. Motion-sensor cameras monitored the sites and recorded animal activity. The trials focused on whether the barriers could prevent animals from crossing into the enclosed railway areas. The results provided evidence about grizzly bears’ responses to active electrified mats.What did cameras reveal about wildlife attempts to cross the electrified matsMotion-sensor cameras recorded 55 individual attempted crossings by 8 different carnivore species during the trials. Parks Canada reported that no grizzly bears entered the exclosure by crossing the electrified mats when those mats were active. The finding suggested that the mats deterred grizzlies from crossing the boundary under the conditions tested. The agency did not describe the 55 attempts as 55 successful crossings.Instead, the figure referred to individual attempted crossings recorded by the cameras. The trials also included fences, jump-outs and wildlife gates, although the page’s reported result specifically concerned grizzlies crossing active electrified mats.Researchers tested a fence with a 90-degree overhang to block bearsA separate Parks Canada project examined a non-electrified fence design intended to stop bears from reaching railway tracks. Researchers tested whether fencing could be modified to keep bears out of high-risk sections of railway or highway. The design had an outward-facing overhang measuring 1 metre and set at a 90-degree angle.Researchers baited the enclosed area and monitored it with motion-activated still and video cameras. No bears successfully climbed over the fence. However, two grizzly bears entered the site by pushing and pulling at a weak point until they made a large hole in the wire.Winter conditions remained a challenge for electrified wildlife barriersReportedly, an electrified fence could provide an additional level of prevention, particularly when bears were strongly motivated by food on the other side. Researchers observed that bears spent more time and effort trying to reach bait in spring and autumn, when natural food was less available. In mid-summer, when food was easier to find, they made less effort to breach the fence. The mats had limits. They had higher failure rates in winter and had not been tested on hoofed animals, called ungulates. Railway testing was needed to assess durability, snow removal, and wildlife responses. The mats, backed by Texas gates, had been installed at highway-fence entrances in Banff and Kootenay National Parks.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: A California facility processes up to 1,000 tons of organic waste daily and turns it into renewable gas; it can also convert sewage sludge into fertiliser
articles.summary: A bioenergy facility in Rialto, California, is giving food waste and sewage treatment by-products a second use by converting them into renewable natural
articles.body: A bioenergy facility in Rialto, California, is giving food waste and sewage treatment by-products a second use by converting them into renewable natural gas and useful soil products. Designed to handle up to 1,000 tons of organic material every day, the Rialto Bioenergy Facility provides an alternative to sending large quantities of waste to landfill. The project also connects waste management with renewable energy production, offering municipalities a way to deal with organic waste while creating a fuel that can enter the existing natural gas network.How the California facility turns organic waste into renewable gasLocated in Rialto, around 50 miles east of Los Angeles, the Rialto Bioenergy Facility was developed to process organic waste collected from municipal waste streams and sewage treatment operations.According to SoCalGas, the facility can accept up to 1,000 tons of material daily. This includes food waste separated from municipal rubbish, liquid waste and municipal biosolids, the material left behind after wastewater treatment. Bringing these different waste streams to one location allows the facility to recover resources that would otherwise require disposal.The project was originally designed, built, operated and financed by Anaergia, a company specialising in technologies that convert organic waste into energy. Its processing system uses anaerobic digestion, a method in which microorganisms break down organic material without oxygen. This process produces biogas, which can then be treated to remove impurities and increase its methane content.The resulting renewable natural gas, commonly known as RNG, can be used in much the same way as conventional natural gas.Sewage sludge also becomes agricultural fertiliserOne of the facility's important features is its ability to process sewage sludge separately from food waste. Municipal wastewater treatment plants produce biosolids during the cleaning of sewage, and these materials need further treatment before they can be put to beneficial use.The California Water Environment Association (CWEA), in its report explains that the Rialto project converts Class B biosolids into Class A fertiliser through a drying process. The plant was also designed to incorporate a technology called pyrolysis, which uses heat to transform dried material into a carbon-rich product known as biochar.According to the facility's project information published by Anaergia, it can process up to 300 tons of dewatered biosolids daily. Its systems are designed to produce up to 30 tons of high-carbon fertiliser and 85 tons of digestate fertiliser per day.The combination of food waste digestion and biosolids processing is what makes the Rialto project different from facilities that concentrate on only one type of organic material.The facility produces energy beyond renewable gasThe plant's operations are not limited to producing fuel for the gas network. It also has a combined heat and power system that generates electricity while recovering heat for use within the facility.The US Department of Energy's CHP Technical Assistance Partnerships at Oak Ridge National Laboratory describes the installation as a 4.6-megawatt combined heat and power project. It uses 4 reciprocating engine units, comprising two 800-kilowatt engines and two 1,500-kilowatt engines.The recovered heat has practical applications in the plant's operations, particularly for heating the digesters and drying biosolids. This helps the facility make use of energy generated during its own waste-processing activities rather than relying entirely on external supplies.The ORNL project profile indicates the total cost of the project is about $185 million. Anaergia’s project information shows the combined heat and power system was commissioned in 2019, with the bioenergy facility itself coming online in 2020.The facility is designed to produce up to 985,000 MMBtu of renewable natural gas annually. The gas is treated to remove unwanted substances before being upgraded to pipeline quality. SoCalGas worked with the developer to establish a dedicated pipeline injection facility, allowing the renewable gas to enter its existing distribution network.This connection means the fuel can be supplied through infrastructure already used to transport conventional natural gas.Why was the Rialto project developedThe facility was developed partly in response to California's efforts to reduce the amount of organic waste sent to landfills. The state's Senate Bill 1383, signed into law in September 2016, established a target of diverting 75% of organic waste from landfills by 2025.Food scraps and other organic materials can produce methane when they break down in landfills. Capturing these materials and processing them through controlled digestion offers an alternative that also creates a usable energy source.SoCalGas identifies the Rialto facility as one of the large-scale projects supporting the state's waste diversion and carbon neutrality goals. It also notes that the renewable gas can be used for transportation fuel, electricity generation and other clean energy applications.The CWEA report highlighted the project's environmental contribution, estimating that its reduction in net carbon dioxide emissions could reach approximately 220,000 metric tons annually. The association compared this reduction with taking around 47,500 cars off the road.The benefit comes from two main activities. The facility produces renewable fuel that can replace fossil-based natural gas, while also diverting organic waste that might otherwise generate methane in landfills.The project receives international recognition and changes ownershipThe scale of the facility's waste-processing and energy recovery operations brought it international attention in 2022. According to the CWEA, the Rialto Bioenergy Facility received the Distinction Award for Wastewater Project of the Year at the Global Water Awards held in Madrid, Spain.The CWEA report described the $185 million development as one of North America's largest organic waste processing projects. At the time, its reported capacity was to convert up to 1,000 tons of wastewater biosolids and landfill-diverted organic waste daily into approximately 985,000 MMBtu of renewable natural gas and agricultural fertiliser.Bioenergy International reported that Sevana Bioenergy acquired the Rialto facility in 2024. The company, which is based in Boise, Idaho, develops and operates large-scale renewable natural gas projects.SoCalGas confirms that the facility is now owned by Sevana Bioenergy and continues to serve the Southern California region.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones | TechCrunch
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones.
articles.body:
CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

“We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”

The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”

Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”

The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

“I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”

articles.title: A batalha na Justiça para apagar homenagem a expoente do racismo científico no Brasil | G1
articles.standfirst: Ação inédita pede a retirada do nome de Nina Rodrigues, defensor de teorias racistas, de hospital público no Maranhão. Justiça determinou a mudança, mas o governo estadual recorreu da decisão.
articles.summary: Ação inédita pede a retirada do nome de Nina Rodrigues, defensor de teorias racistas, de hospital público no Maranhão. Justiça determinou a mudança, mas o governo estadual recorreu da decisão.
articles.body:
Ação na Justiça está tentando retirar o nome de Raimundo Nina Rodrigues de hospital em São Luís do Maranhão — Foto: Gilson Ferreira/Governo do Maranhão

As homenagens a Raimundo Nina Rodrigues no Brasil são múltiplas. O nome do médico legista maranhense batizou o hospital psiquiátrico de São Luís do Maranhão; um município de 14 mil moradores no mesmo Estado; o Instituto Médico Legal de Salvador, na Bahia; uma rua nobre na zona sul do Rio de Janeiro, além de vários outros logradouros espalhados pelo país.

No bairro carioca do Jardim Botânico, a placa da Rua Nina Rodrigues descreve a biografia do maranhense que morreu há 120 anos em letras miúdas: "1862-1906. Médico, catedrático de medicina legal, criminalista, sociólogo, etnólogo, folclorista."

Mas silencia sobre o ideário de Nina Rodrigues, que foi um expoente do racismo científico no Brasil na virada do século e defendia hierarquias raciais – argumentando, por exemplo, com base em estudos craniológicos, que "raças inferiores" como a negra e indígena teriam propensão à criminalidade ou violência.

Em São Luís, uma ação popular inédita está lutando na Justiça para que o Estado do Maranhão retire o nome desta figura histórica do Hospital Psiquiátrico Estadual Nina Rodrigues, pedindo a anulação do ato administrativo que batizou o hospital na década de 1940, sustentando que a homenagem seria um ato lesivo ao princípio constitucional da moralidade administrativa.

Em janeiro, a ação obteve vitória na primeira instância, com sentença determinando a nulidade do ato administrativo que denominou o hospital e a retirada do nome de Nina Rodrigues.

O Estado do Maranhão recorreu, e o julgamento na segunda instância está previsto para o próximo dia 10 de dezembro, em sessão colegiada na Segunda Câmara de Direito Público, no Tribunal de Justiça do Maranhão.

Thiago Cruz espera que a ação gere um precedente judicial importante em debates de reparação histórica — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Autor da ação, o advogado Thiago Cruz defende que hospital psiquiátrico estadual – equipamento público de referência que atende a pacientes de mais de 220 municípios maranhenses – não merece permanecer associado a "um dos principais expoentes de teses eugenistas e raciais" no Brasil. Isso no Estado que tem a terceira maior proporção de pretos e pardos no país, equivalente a 79% da população.

"Foi uma conquista", diz à BBC News Brasil sobre a decisão na primeira instância. "A sociedade de São Luís é muito conservadora, e recebemos diversas notas de repúdio pedindo a improcedência da ação, mas ela gera um precedente judicial importante no debate de justiça histórica e de transição", comemora.

Em Salvador, o nome do Instituto Médico Legal Nina Rodrigues também foi colocado em questão recentemente, embora sem produzir efeitos concretos até hoje. Em 2022, a Defensoria Pública da Bahia recomendou que o governo estadual mudasse o nome da unidade como forma de combater o "racismo institucional." De acordo com o Departamento de Polícia Técnica, ao qual o IML está subordinado, o pedido está sob análise da Procuradoria Geral do Estado da Bahia.

As iniciativas refletem um movimento mundial de questionar homenagens a figuras históricas racistas ou ligadas ao passado da escravização, inspirado em exemplos como o Black Lives Matter, que gerou mobilização global durante a pandemia.

"É um movimento de reparação histórica, que busca desnaturalizar heróis ou grandes nomes de pessoas homenageadas e entender quem elas foram efetivamente", descreve a historiadora Ynaê Lopes dos Santos, professora de História da América da Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF). "No caso do Nina Rodrigues, um dos maiores representantes do racismo científico no Brasil, isso é fundamental."

Rodrigues defendia que negros e indígenas eram inferiores biologicamente — Foto: Domínio público

Raimundo Nina Rodrigues nasceu em 1862 em Vargem Grande (MA). Dividiu os estudos de medicina entre a Bahia e o Rio de Janeiro, onde se formou em 1888, estabelecendo-se depois em Salvador.

Tornou-se referência como médico legista, psiquiatra e acadêmico na Primeira República, época em que essas categorias se consolidavam e se aproximavam de políticas públicas, e o Brasil acabara de abolir a escravidão. Seu círculo de influência gerou um grupo de médicos designado Escola Nina Rodrigues.

Sua formação foi fortemente vinculada ao racismo científico, ideologia que, segundo Ynaê Lopes dos Santos, prevalecia no Ocidente à época, com grande influência do médico e criminologista italiano Cesare Lombroso, também eugenista.

Rodrigues considerava que negros e indígenas eram inferiores biologicamente, e que a mestiçagem levaria à "degenerescência". Chegou a defender a existência de dois códigos penais separados, contrapondo-se ao Código Penal de 1890 (o primeiro da República) por considerar que as raças humanas tinham predisposições distintas para determinados crimes, e, portanto, a imputabilidade também deveria ser diversa.

"Como a seu ver os negros nasciam com uma condição biológica que os levava a cometer determinados crimes, ele defendia que a pena deles não podia ser igual à pena de pessoas brancas. Deveria ser menor, porque eles estariam indo ao encontro de sua natureza", descreve a historiadora.

"E se negros eram mais afeitos a roubos, então a polícia iria sempre olhar com mais cuidado para eles. Isso era algo muito divulgado, e infelizmente vivemos os resquícios disso até hoje."

Foto de 1903 mostra Laboratório de Anatomia Médico-Cirúrgica da Faculdade de Medicina da Bahia; Nina Rodrigues está registrado como uma das pessoas presentes na imagem, mas não há indicação de qual dos homens retratados ele seria — Foto: Arquivo Nacional

Na sociedade em São Luís, a ação judicial pedindo a retirada da homenagem ao maranhense gerou protestos entre associações de intelectuais. Notas de repúdio vieram do Instituto Histórico e Geográfico do Maranhão (IHGM), da Academia Maranhense de Letras e da Associação Maranhense de Psiquiatria, destacando a importância das contribuições de Nina Rodrigues e seu pioneirismo em diversas áreas de estudos, da antropologia criminal à medicina legal e estudos afrobrasileiros.

O IHGM participou da ação popular como amigo da corte (amicus curiae), contrapondo-se à mudança de nome do hospital ao lado do réu, o Estado do Maranhão. Em carta-manifesto, conclamou intelectuais maranhenses a "cerrar fileiras pela preservação da memória maranhense e nacional" e defender a manutenção da homenagem a Nina Rodrigues.

Opositores acusam a ação de "revisionismo histórico", e defendem que a atuação de Rodrigues seja vista à luz das ideias vigentes na sua época.

O juiz Douglas de Melo Martins, que julgou o caso na primeira instância, considera essa visão uma crítica "muito rasteira".

"Muito do que nós temos de racismo, que sobrevive com força nos dias atuais, vem da nossa incapacidade de reavaliar uma visão completamente errada de mundo que predominou no passado", diz Martins, que é juiz titular da Vara de Interesses Difusos e Coletivos de São Luís.

"Essa visão não deixou de existir. E quando o poder público mantém homenagens desta natureza, ele está fomentando, fortalecendo, reproduzindo esta mesma visão, que se projeta no tempo graças a esta homenagem", argumenta.

Em entrevista à BBC News Brasil, ele destaca que a ação é inédita.

"É o primeiro caso em que um processo judicial discute a eventual retirada de homenagem por ente público a uma figura histórica que tenha alguma associação com o racismo."

Na sentença, o juiz ressalta que a mudança do nome do hospital não representaria "ataque individual ao médico", e sim um dever do Estado "de se desvincular de um projeto ideológico racista". Ele remete à Constituição Federal e a tratados internacionais firmados pelo Brasil no combate ao racismo, defendendo medidas afirmativas para efetivar uma justiça de transição e enfrentar "as repercussões ainda presentes do escravismo, do racismo e da eugenia na sociedade brasileira".

Martins espera que a sentença mostre que o Poder Judiciário está preparado para agir quando o Executivo se omite. Ele prevê que o caso possa chegar ao STF, o que seria uma "oportunidade" para a corte firmar entendimento no tema.

Apesar de acatar a mudança de nome, a sentença negou o segundo pedido feito na ação popular: que o hospital fosse rebatizado em homenagem a Juliano Moreira, considerado um dos fundadores da psiquiatria no Brasil.

O juiz entendeu que a escolha do novo nome seria competência do Poder Executivo, mas recomendou que o pedido em prol de Moreira fosse considerado, destacando a importância do médico baiano, que era negro, na humanização do tratamento de doenças mentais e no combate ao racismo científico.

No recurso, o Estado do Maranhão sustenta, por meio da Procuradoria-Geral do Estado do Maranhão (PGE-MA), que o ato administrativo que nomeou o hospital nos anos 1940 passou há muito o prazo de 5 anos de prescrição previsto pela Lei da Ação Popular.

Argumenta que a via da ação popular é inadequada para gerar ao Estado uma "obrigação de fazer" (referindo-se ao pedido de trocar o nome do hospital e renomeá-lo Juliano Moreira); e que o autor não teria demonstrado "lesividade à moralidade administrativa". Por fim, afirma que ação viola a separação de poderes por interferir em uma função do Executivo, descrevendo-a como "um caso clássico de ativismo judicial".

Consultada pela BBC News Brasil, a PGE-MA afirmou em nota que, caso a sentença seja confirmada e após trânsito em julgado, "a decisão judicial será devidamente cumprida pelo Estado".

A Procuradoria afirmou ainda que "não compactua com quaisquer práticas discriminatórias, sendo imprescindível distinguir esse posicionamento institucional das teses técnico-processuais formuladas na defesa judicial do Estado em caso concreto, sobretudo quando tenham foco central em questões formais do processo."

Rua em área nobre do Rio de Janeiro também homenageia o médico legista — Foto: Júlia Dias Carneiro/BBC

Advogado responsável pela ação, Thiago Cruz tem 33 anos. Nasceu em Codó, no interior do Maranhão, e se mudou para São Luís na infância. Teve a ideia de propor a ação após assistir a Holocausto Brasileiro, documentário baseado no livro homônimo de Daniela Arbex sobre as atrocidades cometidas no Centro Hospitalar Psiquiátrico de Barbacena, conhecido como Hospital Colônia, em Minas Gerais, nos anos 1960-80.

O incômodo com a série levou Cruz a refletir sobre o hospital psiquiátrico de sua própria cidade.

"É uma piada de tão mau gosto você ter o nome de uma figura racista em uma instituição psiquiátrica", afirma.

Cruz decidiu processar o Estado do Maranhão com uma ação popular, um instrumento judicial previsto pela Constituição que permite a qualquer cidadão recorrer à Justiça para anular atos lesivos a bens coletivos, desde que esteja em dia com seus direitos políticos. Apresentada em abril de 2024, a ação lhe deu uma nova projeção.

"Aqui em São Luís, eu sou basicamente um azarão. Ninguém me conhecia, eu não sou apadrinhado político de ninguém. Quando teve a primeira audiência pública, muita gente perguntava de onde eu tinha surgido", diz o advogado, que é militante em iniciativas de luta pela terra e atua em coletivos em defesa de movimentos sociais, trabalhadores informais, comunidades indígenas e quilombolas.

O advogado espera que o caso reverbere nacionalmente e abra caminho para "a retirada do nome de figuras racistas, generais e pessoas que não compactuam com o ideal democrático" de edifícios e logradouros públicos.

Ele destaca a importância da nota técnica que a Defensoria Pública da União (DPU) elaborou em janeiro de 2025 a partir da ação, fazendo recomendações para casos no país todo.

No parecer, a DPU considerou a retirada do nome de "pessoas associadas ao escravismo, racismo e eugenia" de locais públicos uma medida "adequada, razoável, atual e justa" em prol da reparação histórica, com capacidade de "produzir efeito reverso ao tributo prestado outrora" e mostrar que o Estado brasileiro "não compactua com a manutenção de deferências carregadas de violência contra grupos vulnerabilizados, em especial contra a população negra brasileira."

O motorista Marcílio Pereira Cruz, 47, mora no Rio, é maranhense e gostou de saber sobre o movimento de mudar o nome do Hospital Nina Rodrigues: 'Acho que é uma homenagem desnecessária' — Foto: Júlia Dias Carneiro/BBC

No "Nina", como o Hospital Nina Rodrigues é chamado por quem o frequenta ou nele trabalha, um funcionário de longa data diz estar acompanhando a luta pela mudança do nome da instituição com interesse – mas afirma ser minoria.

"As pessoas aqui dentro estão muito por fora. Tem gente que diz 'ah, mas por que vai mudar de nome?', sem nem saber quem foi Nina Rodrigues", diz o funcionário, que prefere não se identificar.

"Eu pesquiso, eu sei que o Nina Rodrigues dizia que o negro tinha predisposição para a criminalidade. Não tem lógica uma instituição que fez a reforma psiquiátrica para humanizar o atendimento ter o nome de um cara que pregava o racismo científico", considera. "Muita gente diz que ele deixou muitas contribuições, mas paciência. As coisas mudaram. As coisas estão mudando."

No Rio de Janeiro, a Rua Nina Rodrigues ocupa um quarteirão bucólico entre a Rua Jardim Botânico e uma encosta que desemboca na Floresta da Tijuca.

O porteiro José Rogério da Silva trabalha em um prédio da rua há 26 anos, desde que migrou da Paraíba para o Rio, e nada sabia sobre o homenageado. "Ninguém se incomoda, ninguém nunca reclamou. Pelo menos o nome é fácil de decorar."

Moradora da rua, a jornalista Christina Martins ficou instigada ao saber, por meio da repórter, sobre a ação judicial para retirar a homenagem a Nina Rodrigues no Maranhão. As reflexões a levaram a escrever uma crônica defendendo a mudança de nomes de ruas do bairro, inclusive a sua.

"Nina Rodrigues me fez pensar: se a cidade é um organismo vivo, por que seus nomes não podem acompanhar o tempo?", escreveu, imaginando novos homenageados para o bairro.

"Vai dar um trabalho danado, mas está na hora de atualizar, inclusive para tirar nomes nefastos que não dizem nada para a gente", diz Martins à BBC News Brasil.

Enquanto a repórter tirava fotos na Rua Nina Rodrigues, foi interpelada por uma velha camionete de entrega. O motorista, Marcílio Pereira Cruz, é maranhense, e gostou de saber da ação para mudar o nome do Hospital Nina Rodrigues no seu Estado.

"Acho que é uma homenagem desnecessária. Ele, por ser uma pessoa que não apoia os negros, não pode ter o apoio de uma instituição que reabilita as pessoas", considera.

"Apesar de que as ruas do Rio estão cheias de homenagens aos maldosos de antigamente... Isso não está certo", disse ele.

Marcílio deu um beijo em seu antebraço, negro, e abriu um largo sorriso: "Amo a minha raça, amo a minha cor!"

articles.title: Seca leva reservatório ao colapso em Pernambuco  | G1
articles.standfirst: Barragem de Jucazinho está com menos de 3% do volume de água; moradores enfrentam longos períodos sem abastecimento e animais sofrem com fome e sede.
articles.summary: Barragem de Jucazinho está com menos de 3% do volume de água; moradores enfrentam longos períodos sem abastecimento e animais sofrem com fome e sede.
articles.body:
Se no Sul o excesso de chuva provocou mortes e destruição, no interior de Pernambuco a seca levou reservatórios à situação de colapso.

O cenário de terra seca tira o ânimo de quem vive em municípios como Surubim, no Agreste pernambucano.

"Há uma semana que chegou água aqui, fazia 30 dias que não tinha chegado. Não só na minha casa, mas nessa região todinha aqui", disse Edivando Arruda da Costa, vendedor.

Seca leva reservatórios ao colapso no Agreste de Pernambuco — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Na zona rural, os animais não conseguem esperar. Um pequeno rebanho tenta encontrar alimento no mato seco. A poucos metros, o gado morreu de fome e de sede.

É como se a paisagem do Sertão tivesse se instalado no Agreste, uma área tradicionalmente mais verde. Tudo seco. As folhas se foram e há pouquíssimo sinal de vida por aqui. E olha que nós estamos a menos de 100 metros do principal reservatório de água da região.

A barragem de Jucazinho é a maior da área. Deveria abastecer 14 municípios, mas o volume de água está abaixo de 3%.

A Agência Pernambucana de Águas e Clima afirma que o fenômeno climático El Niño agravou o problema de abastecimento.

"O El Niño começa a incidir e diminui as chuvas nessa região e faz com que os reservatórios diminuam a sua capacidade de armazenamento. Com isso, passa a comprometer tanto a qualidade quanto a disponibilidade de água para distribuição", explicou Danilo Barros, supervisor de monitoramento hidrológico da Agência Pernambucana de Águas e Clima.

Das 99 barragens em Pernambuco, 31 estão com menos de 10% da capacidade. Cinco operam com menos de 1%. E sete não têm um pingo d'água sequer.

A companhia de saneamento declarou que fez ajustes emergenciais para buscar garantir a chegada de água às casas.

"Conseguimos fazer, com os investimentos que vêm em andamento, a interligação da Adutora do Agreste em tubulações que já existem e conseguem mitigar esses efeitos das secas do Agreste Setentrional", ressaltou Flávio Coutinho, diretor de produção e planejamento operacional da Compesa.

Só no entorno de Jucazinho, 800 mil pessoas sofrem com a situação de colapso no reservatório.

Dona Maria do Amparo e seu Manoel moram na região' há quarenta anos e dizem que estão com água contada até para o básico.

"Um litro de dágua para duas pessoas. Porque ninguém pode tomar banho como está. Porque se tomar minha filha, pronto, lascou tudo", disse Maria do Amparo de Lima Félix, agricultora aposentada.

"Restinho só de beber e cozinhar. Já foi da chuva que caiu da bica aqui dentro", comentou Manoel João Félix, agricultor aposentado.

Os dois criam cinco carneiros, que sobrevivem com a água possível.

"Preta, grudenta. Os bichinhos têm que beber isso, que não tem condição de trocar e botar outra", afirmou Manoel.

Em Tupanciretã, o vendável tombou carretas e atingiu cerca de 5 mil casas; 60 pessoas ficaram feridas. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

articles.title: Living to 1,400 could be possible with AI. And that's a conservative estimate, Nick Bostrom says.
articles.summary: Former Oxford professor Nick Bostrom says superintelligent AI could unlock antiaging breakthroughs that help humans live for over a millennium.
articles.body:
Nick Bostrom says AI could help humans live 1,200 to 1,400 years by eliminating aging.

The former Oxford professor says safe superintelligence could unlock breakthroughs in biomedicine.

Bostrom says that delaying AI development means that millions of people die each year.

Dreaming of eternal life? The founder of the Future of Humanity Institute thinks AI could help.

Nick Bostrom , a Swedish philosopher and former Oxford professor, said on an episode of the A16z show released on Thursday that humans could one day live for more than a millennium if AI could unlock breakthroughs in biomedicine and antiaging research that radically extend human lifespans.

"If you think about what our life expectancy would be if we weren't aging, it's something on the order of, you know, 1,200, maybe 1,400 years or so," Bostrom said.

"And that maybe is quite a conservative lower bound, because in this situation you might also have other ways of reducing other mortality risks, like accidents and so forth," he added.

Bostrom studies human enhancement and emerging technologies. At Oxford, he founded the Future of Humanity Institute in 2005 as a multidisciplinary research group, which eventually closed down in 2024.

Bostrom's comments come as AI safety has become an increasingly debated topic, with many researchers calling for AI development to be slowed to address alignment issues and to establish proper guardrails to keep advanced AI aligned with human interests.

Bostrom said the trade-off between developing AI quickly and ensuring its safety is complicated.

"I think that's only one of many different considerations that would come into an all things considered evaluation here," he said. "On the one hand, you might think that if you took some extra time with this AI transition, maybe we could build AI more safely."

"So you might think that if we spend more time doing AI alignment research, the existential risk from developing AI goes down at some rate," Bostrom added. "And then on the other hand, every year that we delay it, we have millions and millions of people dying."

articles.title: Colorado researchers rolled hay bales containing tiny parasitic wasps into wheat fields to fight an insect blamed for $70 million in annual losses; the team is testing whether nature can protect crops
articles.summary: The failure of a crop is an incredibly distressing occurrence for farmers, especially those who depend on it for their livelihoods.
articles.body: The failure of a crop is an incredibly distressing occurrence for farmers, especially those who depend on it for their livelihoods. But what if the answer to protecting a crop from an insect infestation was not another pesticide, but a little helper that could be brought into the field in a bale of hay? The wheat stem sawfly is notorious for damaging wheat plants by laying its eggs inside their stems. But researchers at Colorado State University are exploring just this possibility. In a fascinating investigation, researchers are trying to find out whether rolling out hay bales carrying tiny parasitic wasps into wheat fields could help keep these destructive sawflies under control.Colorado State University's news report by Jayme DeLoss notes that the wheat stem sawfly has been responsible for an estimated $70 million in direct and indirect losses every year in Colorado. The insect has spread across the state's Eastern Plains, affecting wheat farms and making it increasingly difficult for growers to protect their harvests. Researchers at Colorado State University, led by associate professor Punya Nachappa, are now investigating several ways to tackle the problem. Nachappa's team has also been conducting annual surveys to study the sawfly infestation in Colorado.The insect hiding inside the wheatInterestingly, despite its name, the wheat stem sawfly is actually a primitive wasp. The problem begins when female sawflies lay their eggs inside wheat stems. Once the eggs hatch, the larvae feed on the soft tissue inside the stems, gradually making their way down towards the soil surface. As they prepare to spend the winter, they cut a notch inside the stem, weakening it.For farmers, the concern is greater given that this damage takes place inside the plant, making it incredibly difficult to tackle. The larvae remain hidden inside the wheat for most of their development, meaning a plant can appear perfectly healthy from the outside even when it has already been affected. By the time the stems weaken and fall over, the grain can become difficult or impossible to harvest.The insect has become a significant problem for Colorado's wheat-growing communities, with some farms experiencing extensive damage. According to a Phys.org report, Alan Linnebur, a Colorado farmer who has been working with Nachappa's team, shared that roughly two-thirds of his family's wheat has suffered from sawfly damage since the infestation began affecting their farm 16 years ago.Bringing in a natural enemyThis is where the tiny parasitic wasps enter the picture. Researchers are studying a group of wasps known as Bracon, which naturally prey on wheat stem sawfly larvae. Unlike the sawfly, which damages the wheat from within, these parasitoid wasps use the pest itself as a host. A female Bracon lays her eggs on a sawfly larva, and once the eggs hatch, the young wasps feed on the larva, eventually killing it.While these beneficial wasps are relatively abundant in Nebraska, their populations have been much smaller in Colorado. Researchers therefore began exploring whether they could introduce them into wheat-growing areas where sawfly infestations were already a problem.After checking that the parasitoid wasps from Nebraska were a suitable genetic match for the populations they wanted to establish in Colorado, Nachappa and her collaborators at the University of Nebraska and the US Department of Agriculture developed an unusual way of transporting them. They placed hay containing the parasitoids into bales and rolled these out across several Colorado wheat fields. The technique has been given the name 'Beneficial Bug Baler'.The idea is to give the wasps an opportunity to emerge and establish themselves in areas where their natural presence has been limited. According to the research team, studies in Nebraska have indicated that parasitism needs to reach around 50% to improve yields in fields affected by the sawfly. Some of the Colorado sites where the wasps have been released are now approaching this threshold, although researchers are continuing to monitor how well the approach works.When fungi become an unexpected allyThe wasps are not the only natural helpers that researchers have come across while studying the problem. In 2023, Nachappa's team made another rather surprising observation when they found that a fungus had infected and killed some wheat stem sawfly larvae.The fungus reportedly belonged to the Fusarium group, which includes well-known pathogens capable of causing serious wheat diseases. However, the strains that the researchers identified appeared to infect the sawfly larvae without harming the wheat plant.The team has also identified six species of beneficial Fusarium associated with the infected larvae. Laboratory and greenhouse experiments have shown that some of these fungi can kill up to 90% of sawfly larvae. Researchers are now evaluating the most promising strains and exploring whether they could eventually be used to treat wheat stubble in fields.There are other approaches being explored as well. Colorado State University's wheat breeding programme has developed varieties with semi-solid stems, which can crush sawfly larvae as they feed inside the plant. But while these varieties help curtail the damage, they can also produce lower grain yields than hollow-stem varieties, which is why researchers are looking for supplementary techniques that could work alongside them.Can nature help protect the harvest?Although the wheat stem sawfly continued expanding its range in Colorado between 2025 and 2026, the overall infestation rate across the state declined in 2026. Researchers believe that extreme drought conditions and several of the control methods being developed may have contributed to this change, although the exact reasons are still being investigated.The team has also observed an increase in naturally occurring parasitoid wasps in some Colorado wheat fields, including locations where they had not been released. But for now, the researchers are continuing to examine how these different approaches can work together, from introducing parasitoids and studying fungi to developing wheat varieties that are better prepared to tackle the infestations.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Hello, Earth! Nasa's Voyager 1 phones home from beyond 16 billion miles
articles.summary: Nasa's Voyager 1 has phoned home from a staggering one light-day away, with a radio signal from the spacecraft taking exactly 24 hours to reach Earth.
articles.body: Nasa's Voyager 1 has phoned home from a staggering one light-day away, with a radio signal from the spacecraft taking exactly 24 hours to reach Earth. The historic transmission, received by flight controllers on Thursday, marks the first time a human-made object has communicated with Earth from this distance, after travelling more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometres) into interstellar space.The confirmation, received on Thursday through Nasa's Deep Space Network, marks another landmark in the nearly 49-year journey of the spacecraft through interstellar space.Voyager 1 crossed the one-light-day distance threshold on Wednesday at 5:16 am EST (10:16 GMT), Nasa said. The signal travelled at the speed of light before being received by antennas near Madrid, Spain, and relayed to the mission team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in California.Announcing the confirmation amid cheers and applause, flight controller Nshan Kazaryan said: “Voyager 1 light-day distance confirmed..After 16 billion miles of exploration, Voyager 1 continues its journey into the unknown."Nasa officials celebrated the achievement, with the agency's science mission chief Nicola Fox highlighting the significance of the spacecraft's continuing journey. "This is such an amazing day," Fox said at a JPL event. Praising the mission team, she added that it was a group "that just continues to let Voyager keep on trekking out there."Fox also underlined the mission's long-term significance, saying, "When's the mission going to end? It's never going to end, even when we can no longer talk to Voyager."Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 has accumulated several historic milestones during its nearly five-decade journey. The spacecraft flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980 before capturing the iconic image of Earth, famously known as the “Pale Blue Dot”, in 1990. It became the most distant human-made object in 1998 and crossed the heliosphere, the Sun's sphere of influence, to enter interstellar space in 2012.The spacecraft is currently travelling at nearly 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kilometres per hour) in the direction of the star Gliese 445, which is around 17 light-years from Earth. At its present trajectory, it is expected to pass within approximately 1.7 light-years of the star in about 40,000 years.However, the milestone comes as the ageing spacecraft faces technical challenges. Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data over the weekend, although its carrier signal continued reaching Earth. Mission controllers are investigating the interruption.Nasa has progressively switched off instruments aboard both Voyager spacecraft to conserve power from their diminishing plutonium-based energy systems. Voyager 1 now operates with two scientific instruments, while Voyager 2 has three.Voyager 2, launched shortly before its twin, entered interstellar space in 2018 and is expected to reach the one-light-day distance in November 2035.Both spacecraft continue to transmit valuable information about an environment never previously explored by human-made objects. As engineers work to restore Voyager 1's science data transmission, the mission remains a continuing effort to extend humanity's understanding of the space beyond our solar system.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: A nuclear blast might be humanity’s best shot at nudging a killer asteroid off course, but scientists at Sandia found that hitting the wrong side could make the push almost five times weaker than planned
articles.summary: The Big Bang, which gave birth to the universe, is one thing, but could a similar cataclysmic event unfold again if an asteroid came racing towards our
articles.body: The Big Bang, which gave birth to the universe, is one thing, but could a similar cataclysmic event unfold again if an asteroid came racing towards our planet? While the thought might sound like something straight out of a science-fiction film, researchers working on planetary defence have been exploring myriad possibilities to prevent such a catastrophe. One of these involves using a nuclear explosion, not necessarily to blow an asteroid into pieces, but to push it away from its predicted path. What new research has found is rather intriguing: even such a powerful intervention could depend on getting one rather important detail right. Which side of the asteroid should be hit?Recently, researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a new simulation that examines how asteroids respond to nuclear-generated X-rays. Their findings suggest that the direction from which the radiation strikes an asteroid could change the effectiveness of its deflection by almost five times. The research, published in the journal Icarus, also highlights how the irregular shapes of these space rocks could make planetary defence a far more complicated exercise than previously understood.Why would scientists use a nuclear explosion to stop an asteroid?The idea of sending a nuclear device towards an asteroid might immediately bring to mind images of an enormous explosion tearing a space rock apart. However, that is not quite what researchers are trying to achieve. The objective is to alter its trajectory just enough to ensure that it does not collide with Earth.One proposed method involves detonating a nuclear device at a carefully calculated distance from an approaching asteroid. The explosion would release an intense burst of X-rays, which would heat the asteroid's surface and cause some of its material to vaporise. When this material is released from its surface, a recoil effect would ensue, giving the asteroid a push in the opposite direction. Even a relatively small change in its movement could become significant over time, potentially allowing the asteroid to pass Earth rather than collide with it.The challenge, however, lies in predicting just how much of a push an asteroid would need. Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in simplified scientific calculations, asteroids have uneven surfaces, ridges, depressions and rather unusual shapes. This means that the same burst of radiation could produce different results depending on where it strikes.Hitting the wrong side could change everythingTo understand this better, physicist Nathan Moore and his colleagues at Sandia National Laboratories developed a new model to study how asteroids respond to X-ray bursts. Their simulations revealed that changing the direction of the radiation could make a considerable difference, even when researchers were working with the same simulated asteroid.In one instance, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimetres per second when the X-rays struck it from one direction. When the radiation came from another direction, the change was just 0.8 millimetres per second. This amounted to a nearly fivefold difference in the resulting deflection velocity.The researchers also found that the effects were not limited to the direction in which an asteroid moved. Its rotation could be affected as well. For another simulated asteroid, the change in rotational speed varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction from which the X-rays arrived. Therefore, an asteroid's shape determines how different parts of its surface receive the radiation, how much material is vaporised and how the resulting force ultimately affects its movement and rotation.A new model that moves beyond spherical asteroidsFor a long time, modelling asteroid deflection involved a difficult compromise. Researchers could either account for the complicated shapes of asteroids or carry out highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both required computing power that was not readily available.Moore and his team worked towards overcoming this limitation by bringing together two simulation systems used at Sandia for different kinds of physical problems. The resulting algorithm is reportedly more than 1,600 times faster than the earlier approach, allowing researchers to study realistic asteroid shapes while retaining a high level of detail in their calculations.The work also builds on an earlier experiment conducted using Sandia's Z machine, which demonstrated for the first time that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material. The next question was whether scientists could use similar calculations to understand how an entire asteroid might behave.With the new model, researchers can use detailed three-dimensional images captured during spacecraft flybys to reconstruct an asteroid's shape. They can then simulate an X-ray burst while adjusting factors such as the strength of the explosion, its distance from the asteroid and the direction from which the radiation arrives. The software also produces heat maps showing how much material could vaporise across different parts of the surface.There is still a long way to goWhile the findings offer a better understanding of how a nuclear deflection mission might work, the researchers are not suggesting that scientists can now confidently redirect any asteroid heading towards Earth.For one, the current model can only account for the breakup of rocks on an asteroid's surface. It cannot yet accurately predict whether the entire asteroid could fracture under the force of an explosion.But there are a lot of practical difficulties at hand. Firstly, the model requires reasonably accurate information about an asteroid's shape from different directions. Secondly, if a potentially dangerous asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, obtaining detailed observations may not be possible in the limited time available. Lastly, even positioning a nuclear device at the ideal distance and on the correct side of an asteroid could pose a challenge of its own.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Titanoboa, la serpiente más grande conocida: medía hasta 14 metros y pesaba hasta 10 veces más que las serpientes más grandes de la actualidad
articles.standfirst: Una especie de la India podría ser su principal rival por la supremacía
articles.summary: Una especie de la India podría ser su principal rival por la supremacía
articles.body: El ser humano tiene pruebas de que, hace varios millones de años, el planeta Tierra estaba repleto de animales, ahora extintos, que superaron en tamaño, ferocidad y características a los actuales. La evolución y adaptación les hizo, o bien desaparecer o bien modificar su cuerpo para sobrevivir. Hace 60 millones de años vivía la Titanoboa, una serpiente de hasta 14 metros. Esta especie vivió en el norte de Colombia y recibía el nombre oficial de Titanoboa cerrejonensis, siendo la primera vez que se tuvieron restos de ella en la década de los 2000. Tardaron unos años más hasta que se tuvo la primera descripción a partir de sus fósiles, encontrados en fragmentos, por lo que los trabajos para saber sobre ella han sido arduos. Los científicos hallaron trozos de vértebras y costillas, además de dientes y cráneos, siendo imposible hasta ahora encontrar un esqueleto completo. Es por esto que determinar su tamaño y peso se ha basado en sus vértebras, ya que a partir de esto se puede reconstruir su tamaño. La estimación es que la Titanoboa medía alrededor de 14 metros y pesaba alrededor de una tonelada, unas 10 veces más que las serpientes más grandes que se pueden hallar en la actualidad. No obstante, tenía un rival: la Vasuki de la India, que medía entre 11 y 15 metros de largo. La Titanoboa vivió en una época en la que los dinosaurios que no descendían de las aves ya se habían extinguido. Se hallaba en las densas selvas húmedas de Colombia, rodeada de ríos, en una zona ahora reconstruida y poblada. Se cree que era una especie semiacuática que, por su tamaño y peso, tenía complicado vivir y cazar fuera del agua, y solía cazar otros peces y animales acuáticos.

articles.title: Archaeologists on a remote Japanese island uncovered the foundations of a mysterious 900-year-old octagonal building, possibly a Buddhist pagoda, beside evidence of roof tiles shipped about 1,000 kilometres from China
articles.summary: The abyss underwater is vast and mystical, it consists of creatures that stay unknown but glow the brightest, microorrganisms that sustain the ecosystem
articles.body: The abyss underwater is vast and mystical, it consists of creatures that stay unknown but glow the brightest, microorrganisms that sustain the ecosystem or metals and elements that are crucial for the world above. The world underwater is a mystery that keeps unfolding with constant efforts of the scientific community. Professor Satoshi Nakazono of Kagoshima International University has been trying to expose one such secret site on a Japanese Island since 2014. He has uncovered ceramics, roof tiles and other objects originating from China and different regions of Japan.There has been discovery of the foundations of an unusual octagonal structure which is suspected to be the remains of a Buddhist pagoda or religious building constructed around 900 years ago. The site is known as the Ōsato archaeological site located on Kuroshima, which is one of the islands of Mishima Village in Kagoshima Prefecture.Within an area of levelled ground which was previously recorded at the archeological site, a new octagonal arrangement has been identified. The absence of the upperstructure, however, has left the archeologists wondering the purpose of this unique building. The structure is approximately 8.9 metres between opposite corners of its upper section. While individual sides measure around 3.4 metres each. The structure also contains a lower section that is wider, measuring between 10 and 11 metres.Connections to ChinaThere have been previous discoveries of imported roof tiles from Ōsato, the recent findings can help in explaining the questions behind them. While the tiles are characteristic of China’s Southern Song period, Kuroshima is the southernmost known location in Japan where this kind of tiles have been found. Other regions which were closely associated with medieval maritime trade between Japan and China, like Hakata and Kyushu have revealed similar tiles.Earlier research, in 2015, made the discovery of tiles made from the same moulds at Ningbo in China. After further research involving chemical analysis of the samples from the two sites, it was revealed that the examples discovered in Japan had also been produced there. This is especially insightful as it implies that the building materials travelled approximately 1,000 kilometres by sea before reaching Japan.The latest research has raised the possibility that these imported tiles might have been used to roof an octagonal religious structure at Ōsato. Further research, if it confirms the usage, will point to not just transport of construction material but the propagation of architectural styles between the two countries.Could the structure be religious in origin?There have been estimations of the structure being religious, specifically of Buddhist origin. This is because octagonal architecture has associations with Buddhist religious buildings in Japan and China, like pagodas and religious halls. After studying the plan and archeological context, Nakazono and his team have made inferences that suggest Ōsato structure may have housed a pagoda or another sacred building. The structure is also placed within an area believed to have held religious significance and the discovery of Chinese-style roof tiles.The structure revealed has been compared with other similar octagonal religious architecture elsewhere in East Asia. Two of them are present in Japan itself- the nine-storey pagoda formerly standing at Hōshō-ji Temple in Kyoto and the three-storey pagoda at Anraku-ji Temple in Nagano. While the comparisons help in finding the origins of the discovery, the true nature remains uncertain.Beyond religion, trade routes revealedKuroshima's location along the maritime routes of southwestern Japan may explain how imported goods found their way to these otherwise small and remote islands of Japan. The ceramics unearthed at Ōsato suggest that its residents were connected to wider trading networks, rather than being isolated from the outside world. Nearby Iōjima also played a role in regional commerce during the medieval period, when it was known for its sulphur trade, an important commodity exported to China.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Anthropic's IPO buyers made $14 billion on day one, second only to SpaceX: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Anthropic's first-day pop handed IPO buyers about $14 billion on paper, second only to SpaceX.
articles.body:
Anthropic and SpaceX ended their IPO debuts with nearly the same pop. They just got there from opposite directions.

Anthropic ( ANT ) closed its first day of trading Thursday at $97.17, 17% above its $83 IPO price. SpaceX ( SPCX ) closed its June debut at $160.95, up 19%.

That left Anthropic worth about $1.27 trillion at the close, based on the 13.09 billion implied shares outstanding on its Yahoo Finance quote page. That's roughly 60% of the $2.1 trillion SpaceX fetched after its first day, according to the Wall Street Journal. Counting options and other stock awards, the fully diluted figure is closer to $1.6 trillion.

The paths are where they split. SpaceX's first trade came in just 11% above its IPO price, and the stock climbed from there. Anthropic opened with a $12 billion trade at $111.50, 34% above its IPO price. Then it cooled off for the rest of the day.

For anyone who got shares at $83, Thursday was a payday. Anthropic sold 980 million shares, raising $81.3 billion in the biggest IPO ever, according to Renaissance Capital.

By the close, those shares were up about $14 billion on paper. Among 21 big US IPOs since 2008, only SpaceX handed its IPO buyers more on day one, at $14.4 billion. Alibaba ( BABA ), the 2014 record-setter, came in a distant third.

"You want a 15% to 20% pop, right? We're sort of in that window right now," Jim Neesen of Connor Group said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

Measured from its first trade, Anthropic's 13% slide was steeper than all but one of the 20 other big US IPOs since 2008. Only Coupang ( CPNG ) gave back more, at 22%. The typical deal finished about 1% below its first trade.

Facebook, now Meta ( META ), slid 9% from its first trade in 2012 and closed barely above its $38 IPO price, before sinking below it in a debut critics called a "faceplant."

"I feel like I'm back in the Facebook days," Ted Mortonson, technology desk sector strategist at Baird, said on Yahoo Finance's live show.

Retail traders piled in on both sides , though net buying trailed SpaceX's pace, according to Vanda Research.

All 12 of the biggest US IPOs since 2008 fell below their first trade within a year. SpaceX is already there. It closed at $138.43 Thursday, 8% below its $150 first trade and less than 3% above its IPO price.

History isn't much kinder. IPOs from 1980 to 2024 returned about 6% on average in their first year, compared with about 11% for similarly sized companies, according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter's data .

articles.title: UCL scientists develop a water-based battery that stores twice as much energy, paving the way for safer batteries
articles.summary: Batteries are a significant part of our everyday lives. We rely on them, from charging our phones to powering our electric vehicles.
articles.body: Batteries are a significant part of our everyday lives. We rely on them, from charging our phones to powering our electric vehicles. But as storing electricity safely, particularly on a large scale, remains a challenge, the question that arises is how we can find safer and more sustainable ways to do so?Researchers at University College London (UCL) have now developed a new chemistry that could make water-based batteries more capable of storing energy while retaining one of their biggest advantages: safety. According to UCL's latest report on November 13, 2026, the research team has increased the energy-storage capacity of iodine, the material at the heart of their battery, by making it possible for it to participate in a reaction with four electrons instead of the usual two. The developed chemistry, published in Nature, with Dr Ruwei Chen as the first author and Professor Guanjie He as the corresponding author, helps address one of the longstanding limitations of aqueous batteries and brings them closer to practical use.Why water-based batteries are attracting attentionLithium-ion batteries are present in almost all major devices in our lives, from our laptops and smartphones to electric cars, and they are also being deployed in large facilities designed to store electricity generated by renewable sources. But the use of these batteries comes with its own great concerns, with the risk of fire heightened and possible environmental impacts from mining materials such as cobalt. It is to address this problem that researchers at UCL made a major breakthrough.A solution: Water-based, or aqueous, batteries use water-containing electrolytes, which are liquids that allow ions to move between the battery's electrodes while charging and discharging. Since the chemistry behind this function is built on water, these batteries are less prone to fire than conventional lithium-ion systems. However, the catch is that, given the low energy density of these aqueous batteries, their practical use can be rather limited, despite being an appealing option. The researchers at UCL tackled precisely this problem.The chemistry behind the breakthroughThe researchers focused on iodine, which has already been explored as a material for aqueous batteries. In conventional iodine-based battery reactions, iodine transfers two electrons during charging and discharging. The team found a way to enable it to transfer four instead, increasing the amount of energy that the material can store through the reaction.This was not simply a matter of adding more iodine to the battery. The challenge was getting the chemistry to work in water without triggering unwanted reactions. One of the forms of iodine involved in the process, known as hypervalent iodine cations, is highly reactive in aqueous environments. Previous approaches attempted to control this by using very concentrated halogen-containing electrolytes, but these could be corrosive, expensive and difficult to manufacture on a larger scale.Instead, the UCL-led team designed a new electrolyte chemistry that manages iodine's reactivity at a molecular level. Some of the molecules in the electrolyte help prevent water from reaching the iodine, while others bind to reactive forms of iodine, helping to keep the chemical reactions under control. This allowed the researchers to work around the need for the highly concentrated, corrosive electrolytes used in earlier approaches.Testing how well the battery holds upThe researchers tested their design in different configurations, such as pouch cells, which were similar in shape to those used in mobile phones and laptops, and coin cells, the small disc-shaped batteries that are typically used in devices with lower energy requirements.The team also examined how the battery performed over repeated charging and discharging cycles. In zinc-iodine batteries, the design retained almost all of its storage capacity even after thousands of cycles.The approach may not be limited to zinc-iodine batteries either. The researchers indicated that it could also be adapted to aluminium-iodine batteries. As reported by UCL, Professor Guanjie He stated, “This research demonstrates how fundamental chemistry and engineering can come together to address long-standing challenges in energy storage.”Future of renewable energyThe potential of the study extends beyond just small electronic devices. Large-scale battery storage is important for making renewable energy sources more reliable, especially since solar and wind power are not always available at the exact same time as electricity is needed.At the centre of most scientific breakthroughs sits the curiosity and desire to address an issue, developing solutions that can help allay concerns in the real world. The scientists at UCL have hit the nail on the head with their new development, possibly designing safe and sustainable battery alternatives that are more viable in the future. As demand for energy storage continues to grow, breakthroughs like this could help bring safer ways of storing electricity a little closer to everyday use.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
