articles.title: Suffolk MP says Grok was designed to make sexualised images
articles.summary: Jess Asato is suing Elon Musk's company after sexualised images of her were created with the tool.
articles.body:
The Grok chatbot tool was designed by Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence to generate sexualised and offensive images, an MP suing the company has said.

Jess Asato, Labour MP for Lowestoft in Suffolk, is suing SpaceXSI for damages after sexualised images and videos, including some depicting her being sexually assaulted, were generated and shared online using the AI tool.

Her claim alleges SpaceXSI's design choices make them responsible for Grok's output, and that the company misused her private information and breached data protection rules.

SpaceXSI previously said users would no longer be able to use the tool to generate sexualised images of real people.

In court documents published earlier this year , lawyers for Ms Asato claimed she was "victimised" after speaking out against the creation of non-consensual deepfake images of women by Grok.

Marie Demetriou KC, for Ms Asato, said the MP had posted on X on 6 January calling on Musk to "understand that using AI to strip women without their consent is sexual assault designed to degrade and humiliate".

In the days that followed, several X users prompted Grok to create "sexualised, intimate, grossly offensive, degrading, threatening, humiliating and/or discriminatory non-consensual images" of Ms Asato, which were disseminated online, the lawsuit stated.

SpaceXSI also had a "spicy mode" service for Grok which resulted in the AI chatbot generating "more sexual" content, with Grok's system prompts containing the instructions "no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content", according to the MP.

After multiple attempts to report some posts, X refused to remove them, stating in March that they did not violate its terms of service, privacy policy or rules.

Demetriou said that while two videos were later removed, six of 21 posts reported in February remained live as of late July.

The company changed its policy regarding Grok's "spicy mode" in January so that it was only available to paying Grok subscribers, she added.

According to the MP, SpaceXSI – formerly known as xAI – filed a defence to the legal action on 30 October in which it admits the chatbot is designed to expand on short user prompts by pulling data from X threads and the wider internet to create deepfakes.

"Grok is not a passive tool at the mercy of its users," Asato said.

"It is engineered and designed to turn a two-word prompt into fake but realistic, degrading imagery."

She is also asking the High Court to order that SpaceXSI "comply with existing laws to make its system safe for all".

It is illegal to create or request a non-consensual deepfake image of an adult in the UK.

"If an AI product cannot be deployed without automating the humiliation of women at scale, it should not be deployed at all," Asato continued.

"I am taking this case forward to establish a clear principle: tech companies must be held accountable for the harm their systems actively generate."

articles.title: After 43 years without a confirmed sighting, a firefly species has reappeared in Virginia and Delaware; one entomologist recognised its quick amber flashes, while researchers say 28 North American species remain lost
articles.summary: Fireflies are magical beings that emit natural flashes of light.
articles.body: Fireflies are magical beings that emit natural flashes of light. A few hundred of them in the night sky looks like stars have come down to the Earth, little twinkles for just enough time to see them and disappears before you can follow them. Yet, it took just one unusual string of amber flashes for an entomologist to recognise a firefly that scientists had not documented since 1983. Its rediscovery in Virginia and Delaware is bringing fresh hope to researchers searching for 28 other missing firefly species across North America.Recently, a firefly species known as the similar firefly (Pyractomena similis) has been rediscovered in the United States. The sighting is special because it was not sighted for the past 43 years, and was last seen in 1983. The species was spotted in Virginia and Delaware in 2026, giving researchers a reason to celebrate their comeback.A familiar summer light with an unfamiliar rhythmThe discovery in Delaware happened during a field survey in June 2026 when Christopher Heckscher, was observing fireflies at Brandywine Creek State Park. He is an entomologist and ecologist at Delaware State University and he noticed an unusual flicker among the familiar flashes. It was a quick, rhythmic sequence of amber lights. Being a keen local observer of fireflies, Heckscher immediately suspected that he had encountered the similar firefly. Its males are known for producing short amber pulses in quick succession, followed by a brief pause before the sequence begins again. The unusual rhythm was enough for him to observe the unexpected in just a few moments.He subsequently examined a specimen under a microscope. The physical characteristics helped him distinguish it from other fireflies. The identification was finally confirmed in July.But Delaware was not the only place where this mystic insect had made an appearance. Earlier, on May 15, an observer named Aljoscha Nern had spotted a similar firefly in Virginia and uploaded the observation to iNaturalist, a platform where nature enthusiasts and researchers document wildlife sightings. A second population was spotted nearby about two weeks later.In all, the species was recorded three times in the eastern United States during spring 2026. The Delaware sighting was particularly important because it was the first confirmed record of the species in the state.Why did it disappear for so long?The similar firefly was historically known from parts of the eastern and southern United States, including areas around Washington, D.C., Maryland, Virginia, South Carolina, Alabama and Mississippi. However, scientists had never studied it extensively, even before its last recorded appearance in 1983. This means there are still plenty of unanswered questions about its behaviour, population size and preferred habitat.Heckscher found the fireflies in a mature meadow filled with shrubs, brush and low-growing vegetation. The area had been allowed to grow naturally rather than being regularly mowed or managed for livestock. The species is believed to favour open fields and meadows close to water. Such habitats may seem fairly common, but naturally growing meadows are becoming less frequent in many landscapes because of regular mowing, agricultural activity and other forms of land management.The discovery suggests that protecting seemingly ordinary patches of nature could be more important than we realise. A meadow that might look untidy to someone maintaining a manicured landscape could actually be providing the perfect home for an insect that scientists have struggled to find for decades.28 other firefly species are still missingA new study published in the Journal of Lost Species, titled Extinguished or overlooked? An examination of lost firefly species of the US and Canada, identifies 28 firefly species that have not been documented in the United States and Canada for at least a decade. That represents approximately 16% of the region's 178 known native firefly species.The researchers, who include scientists from conservation organisations and academic institutions, are trying to understand whether these insects have genuinely disappeared or have simply escaped scientific observations. According to the research, nine species from a list of missing fireflies compiled in 2024 have been rediscovered. Targeted scientific surveys were condudcted to spot the fireflies in this list. This was complimented by people exploring nature and sharing their observations online.The little lights need darker nightsFireflies are sensitive tiny creatures whose survival depends on a surprisingly specific combination of environmental conditions. They are not really flies, rather, they belong to the family of beetles known as Lampyridae. The emission of light is because of a chemical reaction between oxygen, a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme known as luciferase. For many species of fireflies, these flashes become the way to find a mate. Their patterns of light become signals for males and females to find one another in the darkness.Unfortunately, modern landscapes are filled with artificial lighting, making it difficult for the natural light of the fireflies to show. Moreover, habitat destruction, pesticides, water pollution, invasive species and climate change all threaten firefly populations.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Screwworm outbreak spreads in US, 73 active cases spark fears of winter surge
articles.summary: Flesh-eating screwworm infestations are rising across the southwestern United States, with 64 cases reported in domesticated animals in November alone, up
articles.body: Flesh-eating screwworm infestations are rising across the southwestern United States, with 64 cases reported in domesticated animals in November alone, up from 34 in October and just three in September. The US department of agriculture (USDA) has confirmed 149 cases since June, raising concerns among ranchers, veterinarians and pet owners as unusually warm and wet weather helps the parasite spread.Experts have also warned that the pest could survive winter in parts of the region.Of the 149 cases reported in domesticated animals, 73 were active as of Thursday, compared with just two at the end of September. The USDA has also confirmed two cases in wild elk.Ranchers fear the numbers could rise further because of a shortage of sterile flies used to control the pest. These flies are bred to prevent wild screwworm populations from reproducing."The swarm has not reached Texas yet," said Susan Storey, a South Texas rancher.The parasite was first detected in a calf in Texas in June, after spreading north through Mexico. More cases were subsequently confirmed in Texas and New Mexico. After a lull, infestations reached Arizona last month. The state now has nine active cases across four counties.Dr Ryan Wolker, Arizona's state veterinarian, said the pest had moved into the state from the south and east."The major contributing factor is the natural progression of the pest and the limited supply of sterile male screwworm flies," he said.Warm, wet weather fuels spreadExperts have linked the recent surge to favourable weather conditions. Rain associated with El Niño has created an environment in which screwworms can spread more easily. Hurricanes Rachel and Polo also brought increased late-season moisture to Arizona and Mexico.The development has raised concerns that infestations could continue through the winter. Veterinarians warned that temperatures in parts of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona may not fall low enough to kill the parasite.This means ranchers, hunters and pet owners will need to remain vigilant for signs of infestation."As this spreads, it just exacerbates the need for more sterile flies," said David Anderson, an agricultural economist at Texas A&M University.USDA steps up efforts to contain pestThe USDA is releasing all available sterile flies across the southwestern US and near Mexico's northern border. The flies are intended to prevent the wild population from multiplying. Sterile males mate with wild females, but the eggs they produce do not hatch.However, officials have acknowledged gaps in the sterile-fly barrier along parts of the US-Mexico border."There was a good bit of Mexico where we didn't have a good barrier of sterile flies to stop that natural progression," said Dr Samantha Holeck, New Mexico's state veterinarian. "Now it's right there at the border — both sides of the border."The agency is also working to expand sterile-fly production. The Army Corps of Engineers is overseeing the construction of a fly-production facility in South Texas, which is expected to open next year.The USDA is also testing genetically engineered sterile flies in Panama. Known as NovoFly, these flies are designed to produce only males. This could potentially double sterile-fly production by eliminating females, which are not useful in eradication efforts.USDA Under Secretary Dudley Hoskins told Reuters that the trials were progressing well."To date, all the signs and signals indicate progress and a strong competitiveness of the NovoFly in the wild," Hoskins said. "The tests so far have demonstrated everything we were hoping they would."The USDA intends to produce NovoFly at the Texas facility, scheduled to open in April, if the tests continue to show positive results. Hoskins cautioned that production would take time to scale up.Cattle imports from Mexico resumeThe USDA restarted cattle imports from Mexico through ports of entry in Arizona and New Mexico in August. The imports had been halted last year as part of efforts to prevent the parasite from entering the US. The suspension contributed to a rise in US beef prices, which reached record highs for consumers.However, Hoskins, Wolker and Holeck said the resumption of imports had not triggered a surge in cases. Mexican cattle undergo multiple inspections for screwworm before entering the US.With infestations continuing to spread and winter temperatures unlikely to eliminate the pest in some areas, ranchers remain concerned about the threat to livestock and other animals."We're all nervous," said John Sewell, owner of a 40-square-mile deer-hunting ranch in South Texas. "You can only hope the USDA plan is working."Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Lenders don't want SpaceX shooting their collateral into orbit. What does that mean for space data centers writ large?
articles.body:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

articles.title: Spanish scientists planted hedgerows on abandoned farmland to restore the woodland area; the study found they increased natural oak regeneration by almost threefold
articles.summary: Abandoned farmland in central Spain could recover woodland more quickly with the help of strategically planted hedgerows, according to a study published
articles.body: Abandoned farmland in central Spain could recover woodland more quickly with the help of strategically planted hedgerows, according to a study published in the European Journal of Forest Research. Scientists found that areas containing newly planted hedgerows supported nearly 3 times as many naturally established holm oak seedlings as comparable strips without them. The findings suggest that relatively small changes to agricultural landscapes can encourage forest regeneration without requiring extensive tree plantations, offering a practical approach to restoring biodiversity in regions where natural woodland recovery is particularly slow.Planted hedgerows accelerated natural woodland recovery in SpainThe study investigated how abandoned farmland in central Spain could be restored to a more natural woodland state. The study investigated various methods to help trees and other woody plants to naturally establish themselves.The researchers worked at the La Nava del Conejo Agroecology and Forest Restoration Field Laboratory, in Valdepeñas, central Spain. The landscape included approximately 150 hectares of hills covered with Mediterranean shrubs and woodland, alongside around 220 hectares of rain-fed agricultural fields.Scientists concentrated particularly on holm oak, a tree found in Mediterranean landscapes. They investigated how often new oak seedlings appeared after cultivation ceased, and whether other measures, such as planted hedgerows and bird-attracting structures, could enhance the process.According to the study, natural woodland regeneration can take decades because abandoned agricultural land does not automatically provide favourable conditions for young trees.Why abandoned farmland struggles to become woodland naturallyOne major problem, the researchers said, was the slow rate of natural regeneration of trees. But there are many environmental factors that can prevent woodland from quickly coming back, even when farming activities end.The study said Mediterranean landscapes are marked by hot summers, seasonal drought, strong sunlight and cold winter temperatures. Rocky or shallow soils can also limit the amount of water and nutrients young plants can reach.Another major difficulty is the limited availability of seeds. Agricultural landscapes often contain large open areas with very few mature trees or shrubs capable of producing seeds. Without nearby vegetation, the natural spread of woodland species becomes difficult.‘Animals have a voice too in the process. Birds, rodents and other wildlife help move seeds around the landscape. For example, magpies can carry and bury acorns, enabling new trees to grow away from parent plants. However, this process may not be as effective where there are limited suitable habitats and natural perching sites.To understand the extent of the problem, the researchers examined a 1.95-hectare field that had been abandoned in 1977. Their observations identified 180 additional holm oaks that had established themselves between 1977 and 2021, representing a regeneration rate of just two trees per hectare each year.What the hedgerow experiment revealed about oak seedlingsThe researchers then compared agricultural field edges with planted hedgerows against similar areas without them. These strips had been left unploughed since 2021, allowing vegetation to establish without further cultivation.The planted hedgerows covered several kilometres and contained 21 woody plant species, including different varieties of Cistus, Thymus and Rhamnus, along with hawthorn and other shrubs.The results showed a clear difference between the two types of land. Researchers recorded 44 naturally established holm oak seedlings in strips containing hedgerows, compared with 13 in strips without them.The annual recruitment rate was 22.7 oak seedlings per hectare in areas with hedgerows, compared with 7.8 per hectare in areas without planting. This meant that the hedgerow sections supported almost three times as much natural oak recruitment.The study suggested that the planted vegetation attracted animals responsible for spreading seeds, particularly magpies. These birds can bury acorns in suitable locations, helping new oak trees establish themselves.Researchers also found that the naturally established seedlings were, on average, around 60.8 metres from the nearest mature oak capable of producing acorns. This supported the possibility that birds played an important role in transporting seeds across the fields.Importantly, the newly planted hedgerow species themselves had not yet begun contributing significantly through natural regeneration because the plants had been established only one or two years before the observations.How bird perches and protective fencing supported regenerationApart from hedgerows, the research investigated whether artificial structures could encourage birds to visit agricultural fields and deposit seeds.Scientists installed wooden posts to provide birds with places to perch. Although camera recordings confirmed that birds, including magpies and black redstarts, used these structures, researchers did not find newly established seedlings around the posts during the short observation period.However, older electrical infrastructure produced a different result. The researchers examined electrical supports and transformers that had been present in the landscape for approximately 50 years. Unlike the supports, the transformers were surrounded by fencing.The fenced transformers supported a much higher concentration of naturally established vegetation. Researchers recorded 224 plants per hectare annually around the transformers, compared with 62.5 around the unfenced electrical supports.The findings suggested that fencing helped protect developing vegetation from disturbance and grazing animals. It also provided birds with additional places to perch and deposit seeds.The research also examined whether individual oak seedlings benefited from protective tree shelters. Although protected seedlings grew somewhat taller, their short-term survival was not significantly improved. Nearly all seedlings survived their first summer, regardless of whether they had protection.In Mediterranean regions where natural recovery can take decades, such measures could provide a relatively simple way to improve the chances of forests returning to abandoned farmland.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: New geothermal startups are betting that they can leapfrog today's leaders to deliver terawatts of electricity nearly anywhere.
articles.body:
Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO 2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO 2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO 2 -cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

articles.title: Amazon communities have a complicated relationship with giant anacondas; a 2025 study explores why some people fear them while others live alongside them
articles.summary: Snakes are often associated with negative connotations.
articles.body: Snakes are often associated with negative connotations. The word itself is frequently used to describe someone who cannot be trusted, a person who has betrayed someone or someone who is considered deceitful. But beyond these familiar associations, snakes have a rather complicated place in human societies. While some people fear them, others have learned to live alongside them, even when sharing their surroundings with one of the world's largest snakes: the giant anaconda.Ancient communities around the world have always had a complex and mysterious relationship with snakes. In some communities, they were feared; in others, they were worshipped as protective creatures. Many of the negative connotations surrounding deceit and betrayal come from the biblical story of Adam and Eve, in which a mysterious serpent manipulated Eve into eating from the Tree of Knowledge, bringing upon them original sin and the downfall of humanity. But there are communities that have never considered these creatures as enemies or outsiders, but rather as fellow passengers on the journey of life and sometimes even as a part of the community, well, not a very friendly one, though.In the floodplains of the Lower Amazon, giant anacondas are more than just enormous snakes lurking in the water. They are also part of local folklore, often associated with mythical serpents such as the Boiuna and the Cobra Grande. But for families living along the river, the relationship with these reptiles is not always shaped by myths and legends. Sometimes, it is as practical as protecting their chickens."Chicken is her favourite dish. If one clucks, she comes," one resident told researchers studying the relationship between local communities and anacondas.A 2025 study published in Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile SciencetitledThe Myth of the Serpent: From the Great Snake to the Henhouse. explored how people living in the Lower Amazon perceive these giant reptiles. It found that while anacondas have a place in local beliefs and traditional knowledge, encounters with them can also create conflict, particularly when poultry and livestock are at risk.Between local legends and everyday encountersThe relationship between humans and anacondas in the Amazon is not a recent one. For generations, riverine communities living in the periodically flooded regions of the Lower Amazon have shared their surroundings with them. Their presence has gradually become part of the region's folklore, with anacondas often associated with mythical creatures such as the Boiuna and the Cobra Grande, both legendary giant serpents in Brazilian folklore.These legends have given the anaconda a place beyond that of an ordinary animal, with some traditional beliefs associating it with spiritual and supernatural powers. However, as researchers Beatriz Nunes Cosendey and Juarez Carlos Brito Pezzuti explain in their 2025 study, the relationship has also evolved through everyday encounters. For communities that live close to these reptiles, sharing the same waterways and surroundings means that encounters are sometimes unavoidable.The researchers explored this relationship across five communities in the Aritapera region of Pará, Brazil, drawing on more than 43 hours of conversations with residents. What emerged was a complicated picture: although people possessed considerable knowledge of anacondas and their behaviour, their perceptions of the snakes were often negative. And increasingly, the conflict was no longer just about folklore or fear. It was about something much closer to home: their chickens.When coexistence becomes complicatedBut not every relationship is harmonious. Living alongside these big creatures has its own challenges, and sometimes it is not harmonious. For the communities studied, these reptiles were not merely creatures of folklore or a familiar presence in the surrounding waterways. Their presence could also become a source of conflict, particularly when anacondas entered areas where families kept domestic animals.For many residents, the conflict is rooted less in the fear of being attacked and more in the losses these animals can cause. The researchers found that the primary reason people killed anacondas was to protect their domestic animals, particularly poultry. In fact, 47.7% of the reported motivations for killing were linked to protecting livestock. Other reasons included personal safety and the search for anaconda fat, while the trade in their skins had also contributed to hunting in the past.Interestingly, fear itself was not the strongest motivation behind these killings. The study found that anger over economic losses played a much greater role, while fear often acted as a deterrent. This was particularly evident in the differences between men and women interviewed: men were more likely to report having killed an anaconda, while some women said that fear had prevented them from doing so.The findings reveal a rather unexpected shift in how these communities view the giant snake. An animal once associated with mythical powers and the legendary Great Snake is increasingly seen through the more immediate concerns of everyday life. For some residents, the anaconda is no longer simply a creature of folklore; it has become a source of economic anxiety.And perhaps this tells us more about human behaviour than about snakes. An animal that occupies a place in local myths and traditional beliefs can also become a source of fear, conflict and economic loss. Yet, this does not necessarily make it an enemy. The study highlights how coexistence is shaped not only by cultural beliefs but also by the everyday realities of the people who share their surroundings with these reptiles. After all, living alongside wildlife is not always about learning to love or fear it, but sometimes about finding a way to share the same world. Whatever becomes worthy of worship because of the benefits it offers is, perhaps, simply a reflection of human nature, whether we are talking about gods or animals.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Anthropic mathematician says he used AI to solve the Riemann hypothesis
articles.summary: Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said Friday he used Claude to solve the Riemann Hypothesis.
articles.body:
A mathematician said on Friday that he cracked one of the biggest problems in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said he used Claude to solve it.

Mathematicians told Business Insider the result hasn't been fully verified yet.

One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI.

Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude.

"I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet.

"If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz , a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale."

Sergei Gukov , a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal."

"This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math."

Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes .

"So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said.

The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers.

The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category.

Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said.

Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time."

Alpöge, who joined Anthropic in 2024, said he actually solved the problem on Sunday, but decided to hold off on announcing it after speaking with CEO Dario Amodei and consulting with other mathematicians.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, went public on the stock market on Thursday. As of Friday afternoon, the price of Anthropic shares has steadily declined.

Alpöge said he didn't want to release "slop" to the public, adding that he still doesn't fully understand the math involved.

Still, he said that as other mathematicians attempt to grapple with the results, Alpöge said he plans to be there every step of the way to help them.

"I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument," he said.

articles.title: A Virginia woman who looks after 27 nest boxes near her home has helped 1,674 baby bluebirds take flight since 2006, checking every box each week from April to July and logging every single egg
articles.summary: Spring is more than just another season; it comes with warmth, familiarity and hope for a better tomorrow after a chilling winter night.
articles.body: Spring is more than just another season; it comes with warmth, familiarity and hope for a better tomorrow after a chilling winter night. With the smell of roses, the shining sun and a cool breeze brushing against your face like a lover's touch, spring has a way of making everything feel alive. When poets say that love is in the air, they were probably talking about spring. But are humans the only ones who get to experience this feeling? The answer is no.For birds, too, spring marks the beginning of a new chapter. As temperatures rise and nature begins to bloom, it also signals the arrival of nesting season for several species. Among them are Eastern bluebirds, whose breeding season brings a familiar sight across parts of the United States: pairs searching for suitable nesting spaces and raising their young.Every spring, when the bluebirds begin looking for places to nest, a Virginia woman sets out on a familiar weekly routine. She checks 27 nesting boxes near her home, keeping track of every egg, hatchling and young bird until they are ready to take flight. It is a commitment she has maintained since 2006, helping 1,674 baby bluebirds successfully leave their nests over the years.As reported by The Northern Virginia Daily, Cathi Morrison, a resident of Virginia's Warren County, has turned her interest in bluebird conservation into a long-running effort involving 27 nesting boxes across the Rockland community. Having started in 2001, Morrison has been monitoring the boxes during the nesting season, checking each one weekly between April and July and documenting every nesting attempt, egg and fledgling. Since 2006, her records have documented 831 nesting attempts, 3,517 eggs and 1,674 fledglings. Her observations are also shared with the Virginia Bluebird Society and Cornell University's NestWatch programme, contributing to wider efforts to understand and protect bluebird populations.Why bluebirds need a helping hand“It's a rough life out there,” Morrison told Ashley Miller of The Northern Virginia Daily, describing the challenges young bluebirds face during the nesting season. According to Morrison, life for young bluebirds can be very unpredictable. While a nesting box may offer bluebirds a safe place to raise their young, survival is far from guaranteed. During particularly hot spells, temperatures inside the boxes can become unbearable for the hatchlings. Prolonged rainfall brings another challenge, making it difficult for adult birds to find enough insects to feed their young.But the weather is not their only enemy. Predators such as snakes and raccoons can threaten eggs and hatchlings, while invasive English sparrows sometimes take over nesting boxes, destroying existing nests and displacing other birds. This is where regular monitoring becomes important, allowing conservationists like Morrison to keep track of nesting activity and identify threats before they go unnoticed.More than just putting up a birdhouseFor Morrison, protecting bluebirds goes beyond simply putting up nesting boxes. Their surroundings also play an important role in their survival. She maintains what she calls a “messy yard”, avoiding chemicals and allowing insects and other forms of wildlife to thrive. Since insects are a major food source for bluebirds, their availability can directly affect the survival of young birds. She and her husband, Woody, are also concerned about declining insect populations and the effects of pesticides, particularly systemic pesticides that can make entire plants toxic to insects.They are what netizens might call a 'power couple', but for a different reason. The couple's interest in protecting wildlife goes beyond bluebirds. They are equally invested in protecting fireflies and other species. Their observations reflect a larger environmental concern: the decline of one species can have consequences for several others, disrupting the delicate relationships that sustain an ecosystem.For Morrison, the work is far from over. With 27 nesting boxes already keeping her busy, she hopes more people will take an interest in monitoring local bird populations and contribute their observations to conservation efforts. She encourages people to install suitable nesting boxes, plant berry bushes, provide natural habitats and avoid unnecessary pesticide use. What began as a casual interest more than two decades ago has grown into a contribution to a much larger conservation effort. And as another nesting season arrives, Morrison will continue her weekly rounds, one box and one bluebird at a time.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Rare alien-like sea creature that packs painful sting spotted on SoCal coast
articles.summary: Their blue-purple coloring can make them easy to confuse with another local visitor.
articles.body:
A venomous sea creature with an otherworldly appearance is turning up on Southern California beaches , and getting handsy with one could leave beachgoers with a world of pain.

Portuguese man o' wars, bizarre blue-and-purple marine animals armed with long, stinging tentacles, have been spotted near Cabrillo National Monument's tide pools and along the beaches of Del Mar and La Jolla, according to UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography .

The sightings are extremely rare in San Diego, prompting scientists to investigate whether warmer ocean waters associated with El Nino are bringing the creatures closer to shore.

"This is an exciting occurrence for this region, and we are grateful to the curious and careful naturalists who reported them," said Linsey Sala, manager of Scripps ' Pelagic Invertebrate Collection.

But beachgoers should admire the strange-looking visitors from a distance.

"While the man o' war's sting is rarely deadly to people, it packs a painful punch and causes welts on exposed skin," the National Ocean Service warned . "Found mostly in tropical and subtropical seas, men o' war are propelled by winds and ocean currents alone, and sometimes float in legions of 1,000 or more."

Despite the painful sting, Sala said there's no need to panic.

"Knowledge is power, and knowing that these gorgeous animals may periodically be here allows us to keep an eye out and aim to avoid touching them while on beach walks or swims," she said.

Known scientifically as Physalia, Portuguese man o' wars are siphonophores, marine animals closely related to jellyfish.

They are also found in places including Hawaii and Australia.

Their blue-purple coloring can make them easy to confuse with another local visitor, the by-the-wind sailor.

But Scripps says man o' wars have gas-filled floats and long, trailing tentacles that set them apart.

Anyone who spots one should keep their hands off. If stung, experts recommend rinsing the area with seawater, carefully removing visible tentacles and immersing the affected skin in hot water until the pain subsides.

articles.title: In 1956, a skeleton was found in an ancient Danish shell dump; 70 years later, fresh analysis suggests the man lived through the shift to farming 6,000 years ago while changing from a seafood-heavy diet
articles.summary: Change can be tough for everyone. Shifting jobs, houses, cities; all are changes we struggle with in today’s day and age.
articles.body: Change can be tough for everyone. Shifting jobs, houses, cities; all are changes we struggle with in today’s day and age. But, 6000 years ago, changes were a bit more severe.For a child growing up on the Danish island of Sejerø around 6,000 years ago, the sea would have been less a scenic backdrop than a pantry. Molluscs could be gathered from the shallows, flatfish and eels caught close to shore, while deeper waters offered larger fish. A man now known as Rødhals Man appears to have grown up on precisely this menu. But the food he ate did not stay the same throughout his life, and that small change may have placed him in the middle of one of prehistory’s biggest transformations.The discovery of the remainsRødhals Man’s nearly complete skeleton was discovered in 1956, when residents digging for artefacts came across human remains in an ancient shell midden at Rødhals, on Sejerø. The midden was essentially a prehistoric food-waste heap of shells, bones and other remains. The skeleton lay beneath an undisturbed layer of shells about 20 cm deep. Archaeologist Ole Klindt-Jensen was sent to document and recover it, reportedly working in the pouring rain.The discovery took decades to become fully understood. Radiocarbon dating placed him near the end of the Mesolithic period, when hunter-gatherer communities were giving way to farming societies. Yet his DNA showed that he belonged to the indigenous Western Hunter-Gatherer population, while earlier analysis suggested that he had relied heavily on seafood. He seemed to belong to an older way of life, even as farming was spreading around him.A study published in the journal Antiquity on November 16, 2026, has taken a closer look at his bones and teeth. By analysing stable isotopes in the remains, researchers could trace changes in the kinds of protein he ate at different stages of his life. The team also refined the radiocarbon dating, accounting for the fact that people who ate a lot of marine food can appear older in radiocarbon tests than they really are. Their revised estimate suggests he died most likely between 3890 and 3770 BCE, when he was around 30 to 40 years old.A shift from sea to landThe results offered the scientists a detailed picture of his diet. As a child, Rødhals Man ate mostly food from the shallow coastal waters around Sejerø, including shellfish, flatfish and eels. From around the age of 11, his diet began to include more fish from deeper waters. During adolescence and adulthood, however, the proportion of protein from land-based sources rose sharply. Seafood remained important, but it no longer dominated his diet in quite the same way.Researchers believe the increase in terrestrial food may reflect contact with the farmers arriving in the region. Sejerø is a small island with limited space for large land animals, while the larger island of Zealand lies around 18 kilometres away. Farming communities had already begun establishing themselves there. Rødhals Man may have travelled between the islands, spent time among farming communities or obtained food from them. His burial also appears to share features with graves associated with early farmers.While isotope analysis can show that more of his protein came from land-based sources, it cannot tell whether that food came from domesticated animals or wild game. He may have spent time hunting and gathering on a larger landmass before returning to Sejerø. The researchers therefore describe farming as a likely explanation, but not necessarily a certainty. What they can say is that his adult diet was unusual for a coastal hunter-gatherer of the period.Rødhals Man, beyond the dietThe rest of his skeleton offers a few more clues about the person behind the label. He stood about 1.55 metres tall, was right-handed and showed no signs of having died violently. His bones suggest he was generally healthy and well-nourished in early life, although traces of inflammation or vitamin deficiency appeared later. Wear around his joints and heels also points to considerable physical strain, possibly from repeated paddling.Rødhals Man did not neatly switch from one lifestyle to another. He remained genetically part of the Mesolithic hunter-gatherer population, and seafood continued to feature in his diet. But he also appears to have incorporated more food from the world of farming, at a time when that world was expanding around him. The researchers identify him as the latest known individual in Denmark with this combination of unadmixed Mesolithic ancestry and a marine-dependent diet.It is tempting to imagine the arrival of agriculture as a clean break, with one way of life simply replacing another. Rødhals Man suggests something messier and more human. People lived through the change, encountered new communities and adapted without necessarily abandoning everything they knew. His bones cannot tell us what he thought of the farmers, or whether he considered himself part of a changing world. But they preserve something almost as valuable: a record of that change taking place over the course of one ordinary life.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Scientists surveying Bolivia's Madidi National Park have confirmed 99 bat species, including seven never before recorded in the country and one potentially new to science, revealing unexpected diversity across forests
articles.summary: While people adore animals, few are not very famous among humans.
articles.body: While people adore animals, few are not very famous among humans. It might be because of their hideous appearance, strange behaviours, being stinky, or maybe they just haven’t gained popularity in the human world. But bats are creatures that are not unknown but infamous, especially after the Covid-19 pandemic. However, their contribution to nature cannot be ignored, which is why detailed studies are conducted to study them extensively.In Bolivia's Madidi National Park, scientists have been listening, watching and looking a little closer. And they have discovered something remarkable. The latest research has documented 99 bat species in a single protected area of Bolivia. Out of these, seven have been recorded in Bolivia for the first time, while one additional bat could represent a species never described by science. The findings, announced by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) on November 16, 2026, place Madidi among the world's richest protected areas for bat diversity.A forest hiding an extraordinary number of batsMadidi National Park and Natural Area of Integrated Management is located in Bolivia and covers nearly 19,000 square kilometres. The nature sanctuary spreads from Amazonian rainforests and tropical foothills to high-altitude regions of the Andes. This distinguishes Madidi, as it contains different climates, vegetation and elevations under one protected area. Thus, the wildlife in the region is extremely varied, with the availability of different habitats in which they can feed, shelter and reproduce.The latest research confirms that the park supports more than two-thirds of Bolivia's known bat fauna. The research found 25 new bat species records that had not been documented in Madidi before. Among them, there were seven that had never previously been recorded anywhere in Bolivia as well. The study also recorded a potentially undescribed species belonging to the genus Histiotus. If further investigation confirms its identity as a new species, Madidi's tally could reach 100 bat taxa.The study, titled ‘Bats (Chiroptera) from Madidi National Park: An Integrative Assessment from Field Surveys, Museum Collections, and Historical Records’, was published in the scientific journal ZooKeys.Listening to the forest after darkBats are nocturnal, often small, and some are particularly difficult to observe using conventional wildlife-survey methods. The research was conducted under the Wildlife Conservation Society's (WCS) Identidad Madidi initiative, which combined several techniques to track these bat species.Field surveys were conducted between 2015 and 2017 across 12 locations, covering elevations ranging from 198 metres to an astonishing 4,814 metres above sea level. Scientists also used nets to capture bats, searched potential roosting sites and employed acoustic detectors to record their ultrasonic calls. These detectors were particularly useful because bats navigate using echolocation, producing sounds generally beyond the range of human hearing.The team captured 820 bats belonging to 69 species. Acoustic recordings revealed another 28 species, including 14 that were detected exclusively through their calls. Combining the field observations with historical records and museum collections eventually produced the confirmed count of 99 species.Bats spread their wings across different forestsMadidi being an extremely biodiverse landscape, the bat diversity was also unevenly distributed throughout the park. While 77 species were documented in the Sub-Andean Amazon Forests, 66 were found in the Pre-Andean Amazon Forests and 49 in the Yungas. The numbers reflect how variation in habitat has an effect on the kind of bat communities present in the region.The researchers also found considerable differences in the composition of bat communities between these ecological regions. This matters because protecting a forest does not simply mean protecting its trees. It means preserving the different environments that allow its wildlife to survive. As Robert Wallace, WCS Bolivia's senior conservation scientist and a co-author of the study, explained, conserving Madidi's biodiversity requires protecting the entire landscape, from the Amazonian lowlands to the high Andes.The potentially new Histiotus species still requires further investigation before scientists can formally establish whether it is new to science. Researchers have also cautioned that differences in sampling effort mean additional surveys are needed to understand the distribution of bat species more completely.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: A second moon for Earth? Meet the asteroid temporarily orbiting our planet
articles.summary: Jupiter has a whole family of moons, Saturn boasts even more, and even our neighbouring Mars has two.
articles.body: Jupiter has a whole family of moons, Saturn boasts even more, and even our neighbouring Mars has two. Earth, on the other hand, has always had just one natural satellite to call its own.But not anymore, at least for a little while. Our planet has found itself a second celestial companion after a tiny asteroid was pulled into its gravitational embrace. The catch? This unexpected guest is only here temporarily and is expected to make its exit in early December.What appears to be an unusual addition to Earth's neighbourhood is a tiny asteroid designated 2026 QQ8, measuring approximately 2 metres (6 feet) across.The asteroid has been temporarily captured by Earth's gravity and is now orbiting the planet as a mini-moon. However, unlike our permanent natural satellite, this rocky visitor is only passing through and is expected to escape Earth's gravitational influence in early December.Matthew Payne, director of the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center, told CNN that the asteroid entered Earth's gravitational influence in April 2026.So, how did Earth manage to capture this tiny space rock? The asteroid was already travelling around the Sun when it approached our planet in April. As it moved closer, Earth's gravitational pull began influencing its trajectory, gradually drawing it into a temporary orbit around the planet. The gravitational interaction also involved the Moon, further influencing the asteroid's movement.Matthew Payne explained to CNN that the object was moving alongside Earth before drifting closer, allowing it to increasingly feel the gravitational forces of both Earth and the Moon. This temporary capture has turned the asteroid into what astronomers call a mini-moon.The asteroid, designated 2026 QQ8, is approximately 2 metres (6 feet) in diameter, making it barely larger than an average adult human. Despite being Earth's temporary companion, it is too small and faint to be spotted with the naked eye. It is also not particularly close to our planet, with its distance reaching approximately 568,000 kilometres at its closest approach during the capture.Unlike Earth's permanent Moon, which has remained in orbit for billions of years, 2026 QQ8 is only a temporary visitor. Once it escapes Earth's gravitational influence, it will continue travelling around the Sun along its own orbital path.The mini-moon was first spotted on August 19/20 by Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky, who initially suspected it could be a piece of space debris rather than a natural asteroid.Further observations using telescopes in Arizona and Hawaii helped scientists establish its natural origin.By early December, it is expected to leave our planet's gravitational grasp and continue its journey around the Sun, leaving Earth with its familiar single permanent moon once again.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: A developer secured approval for 26 houses on 94 wooded acres in Massachusetts in 2023; now a land trust is close to buying the site for about $2 million to protect its wetlands and link surrounding forests
articles.summary: A 94-acre woodland in Gloucester, Massachusetts, which was approved for a 26-home housing project in 2023, could soon become a protected conservation area.
articles.body: A 94-acre woodland in Gloucester, Massachusetts, which was approved for a 26-home housing project in 2023, could soon become a protected conservation area. Essex County Greenbelt, a regional land trust, is close to buying the property to preserve its wetlands, forests and wildlife habitat and connect it with nearby protected land.The property, known as Magnolia Reserve, is next to Ravenswood Park, a 600-acre conservation area. It also borders other protected land owned by Greenbelt and the City of Gloucester. Protecting the site would create a larger connected area for wildlife and give visitors access to a network of walking trails.According to a report by Cape Ann Current, most of the money needed for the conservation project is now in place. A city official said on November 16 that the sale was expected to close within weeks. However, the purchase is not final, and some city funding approvals are still pending.How 26 homes were approved on the propertyThe original housing proposal was submitted by How-Mag LLC, working for Howland Development Co., in October 2022. Gloucester's Planning Board approved it unanimously on October 5, 2023. The plan included 13 duplex buildings, with two three-bedroom homes in each building. Four of the 26 homes were to be set aside as affordable housing. It also included a road from Magnolia Avenue, a shared septic system and three stormwater basins to collect rainwater.More than 80% of the property was to remain open space, with public trails. The plan also proposed a permanent legal restriction to protect that open land from future development. But the Planning Board's approval was not enough to begin construction. The developer still needed a wetlands permit from the city's Conservation Commission. That permission was never granted.Wetlands and wildlife raised concernsThe main concern was a cedar swamp near the proposed construction area. According to Cape Ann Current, scientists working for the developer told the commission that the swamp functioned as a vernal pool. These are seasonal pools where frogs and salamanders can lay eggs. Scientists reported finding wood frog and spotted salamander eggs at the site.The commission questioned whether the proposed stormwater basins were too close to the wetland. The basins were meant to collect and filter rainwater from the development's road. The city's conservation agent said some did not meet the required distance from the wetland.There was also disagreement over a stream on the property. Under state rules, a stream that flows throughout the year has a protected area extending 200 feet on either side. The developer argued that the stream dried up. However, the photographs submitted as evidence were taken during a period when a drought had begun. The commission did not accept them as sufficient proof.In February 2024, the commission voted 6-0 to appoint an outside reviewer to examine the project's effect on the habitat. The review raised concerns about the plan to rebuild habitat near the swamp. The developer later proposed measures such as weekly checks by scientists during the breeding season.The last full discussion of the 26-home proposal took place in April 2025. The question about the stream remained unresolved, and no wetlands permit was issued.A change in plansThe four lots making up the property were sold for $1 million on September 22, 2025, to a company called Magnolia Reserve of Gloucester LLC, according to city property records.At a Conservation Commission meeting in October 2025, a representative of the new owner said he would probably withdraw the 26-home proposal and consider a smaller development farther from the wetland.In May 2026, Greenbelt presented a different plan: buying all 94 acres and protecting them as conservation land. The Gloucester Conservation Commission voted on May 20 to support the purchase and the property's permanent protection.Planning Director Gregg Cademartori told the commission that the city had tried to protect the same land with partners about 15 years earlier but had not succeeded. Commission member Dave Sargent thanked him for continuing to pursue the effort.Under the new proposal, Greenbelt would own and manage the property. The city would hold a legal conservation restriction to prevent future development. Greenbelt also plans to create marked trails connecting the land with Ravenswood Park, the city's water supply lands and its Nelson Reservation.Where the $2 million funding will come fromThe conservation project has a funding target of about $2 million. According to Greenbelt's funding list reported by Cape Ann Current, the money is expected from five sources:$500,000 from Mass Audubon Catalyst Funds, already awarded.$500,000 in foundation support, which the Community Preservation Committee chair said had been approved.$425,000 from a state LAND grant, awarded to Gloucester on October 7. The City Council still needs to accept it.$300,000 from Gloucester's Community Preservation Act funds, for which a committee vote is scheduled on December 14.$275,000 through Greenbelt's fundraising efforts.The city's application lists the total project cost as $2,021,600. The amount Greenbelt has agreed to pay the current owner has not been made public, according to Cape Ann Current.The purchase still needs some public funding decisions. The city council must review and accept the state grant, while the Community Preservation Committee is due to vote on the proposed $300,000 contribution. The wetlands application for the housing project also remains open. The Conservation Commission's November 18 agenda listed a request to move the next hearing to December 16.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: NASA is offering $1 million to anyone who can solve one big problem standing in the way of building a human settlement on the Moon
articles.summary: We have spent decades imagining what life on the Moon might look like.
articles.body: We have spent decades imagining what life on the Moon might look like. Since the day Neil Armstrong took humanity's first steps on the lunar surface in 1969, space agencies have been dreaming of a day when humans might actually be able to live there. While conversations about space exploration in recent years have increasingly shifted towards Mars, the idea of establishing a permanent human settlement on the Moon is far from forgotten. But before anyone can think of moving in, there is one rather important question to answer: how do you actually build a home on the Moon? NASA is now turning to student innovators, offering $1 million in prizes to those who can help solve some of the biggest challenges standing in the way.According to NASA, the initiative, called the Moon Base Challenge, invites student teams from high schools and post-secondary institutions across the United States to develop innovative solutions that could help make a permanent human presence on the Moon possible. With $1 million in total prizes at stake, the competition focuses on six key areas of lunar settlement, including power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks and astronaut safety.Carlos García-Galán, manager of NASA's Moon Base Program, said in the official announcement of the Moon Base Challenge on November 8: “As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there.” He further explained: “Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.”What NASA wants students to solveWhile announcing the challenge at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.”Through the programme, NASA wants to bring in different approaches and perspectives to address a long-standing question. Building a settlement on the Moon is considerably more complicated than transporting construction materials and putting up a few habitats. From surviving extreme temperatures to ensuring astronauts have enough oxygen and electricity, a lunar settlement presents challenges that are very different from those we face on Earth.According to NASA, the Moon Base Challenge focuses on six key areas:1. Generating and storing powerOne of the biggest challenges is ensuring a continuous supply of electricity. A lunar settlement would need power for lighting, heating, communication and essential equipment. However, lunar nights can last approximately 14 Earth days, making it necessary to develop reliable energy storage and generation systems that can keep the base running even without sunlight.2. Building habitats on the MoonBuilding a home on Earth is one thing, but constructing one on the Moon is an entirely different challenge. Transporting construction materials from Earth would be expensive, which is why NASA is interested in innovative building techniques, materials and the possibility of using resources already available on the lunar surface.3. Developing life-support systemsHow would astronauts breathe, obtain drinking water and maintain a comfortable living environment so far away from Earth? A permanent settlement would require systems capable of supplying breathable air, recycling water and maintaining suitable living conditions while reducing dependence on regular deliveries from Earth.4. Finding ways to move across the lunar surfaceA lunar settlement would need more than stationary habitats. Astronauts, robots and cargo would have to travel across uneven terrain to transport equipment and explore the surrounding landscape. NASA wants students to consider mobility solutions that can withstand the Moon's challenging surface conditions.5. Establishing reliable communication networksEven a minor communication failure could create serious problems for astronauts working on the Moon. A permanent base would require reliable networks connecting astronauts, equipment and mission control on Earth, allowing them to coordinate operations and exchange information across the lunar surface.6. Protecting astronauts from lunar hazardsPerhaps the most important consideration is keeping astronauts safe in an environment without Earth's protective atmosphere and magnetic field. Radiation, micrometeorites, extreme temperatures and abrasive lunar dust all pose risks. Students are therefore being encouraged to explore technologies that can protect astronauts and make long-term lunar operations safer.How can students enter the competition?Students interested in participating must form teams of two to five members and register through NASA's STEM Gateway and the Moon Base Student Challenge website provides the compitittion's rules, guidance and updates. Each team must also have an adult coach who will guide the participants and help with administrative requirements. The competition has separate divisions for high school and post-secondary students, with participants required to be enrolled in eligible US-based educational institutions.Registration is open until January 25, 2027. Once registered, teams will be expected to develop a concept addressing one of the six technical categories and submit a five-to-seven-page proposal by February 22, 2027. Teams selected for the final phase will then prepare a video presentation and slide deck outlining their proposed solutions.Important dates to rememberCompetition milestoneDateRegistration closesJanuary 25, 2027Initial project submissionFebruary 22, 2027Finalists announcedMarch 11, 2027Final submission deadlineApril 19, 2027Winners announcedMay 6, 2027For now, a permanent human settlement on the Moon may still sound like something pulled from the pages of science fiction. But turning that vision into reality will require more than ambitious space missions and advanced spacecraft. It will depend on solving the everyday challenges of living beyond Earth, from finding reliable sources of power to ensuring astronauts can breathe, move and work safely. And if NASA's latest challenge is any indication, some of the ideas that eventually make lunar life possible could come from students who are only beginning their journeys in science and engineeringFearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Scientists flew drones through humpback whales' breath off Canada and sequenced entire genomes without touching the animals, using 58 samples from 26 whales and finding three previously unknown genetic variants
articles.summary: The University of St Andrews has developed a simpler and less invasive way of collecting DNA samples from whales using small drones to gather what is
articles.body: The University of St Andrews has developed a simpler and less invasive way of collecting DNA samples from whales using small drones to gather what is commonly known as whale snot. In a news report published on November 17, 2026, scientists successfully sequenced whole whale genomes using samples collected off the coast of British Columbia, Canada.The team devised a method to sequence whole nuclear and mitochondrial genomes specifically through the whales' exhaled breath. This is the first time whole genomes have been sequenced using whale blow samples collected without invasive physical interventions such as darts or biopsies.The findings, published in the journal Molecular Ecology Resources, offer a new way of studying whale populations and their genetic makeup through a method that could make genetic research a far less intrusive and more practical scientific process.Collecting DNA from a whale's breathWhen humpback whales surface after spending time underwater, they forcefully exhale through their blowholes, releasing a mixture of air and water droplets. This is commonly referred to as a whale blow. What can look like nothing more than a burst of spray above the ocean's surface can actually contain biological material from the animal itself, including DNA that researchers are interested in studying.For the examination, scientists attached sterile Petri dishes to small commercially available drones, which were then flown through the whales' exhalations as the animals surfaced. The droplets landed on the dishes, allowing the researchers to retrieve a total of 58 samples between July and September in 2022 and 2023. These samples were collected without using darts or taking tissue directly from the whales and was tested on 26 individual humpback whales in the Kitimat Fjord System, within the territory of the Gitga'at First Nation in northern British Columbia.During each sampling attempt, the drone was flown through between one and five breaths from the same whale during a surfacing event. More than one-third of the samples were collected by launching the drones directly from land. There were also precautions in place to minimise disturbance. Scientists avoided sampling whales that were resting, and if an animal showed any reaction to the drone, the flight was stopped. When several whales were swimming together, researchers targeted the individual positioned furthest upwind to reduce the possibility of collecting mixed genetic material from more than one animal.Studying the DNA more closelyOne of the most interesting findings was just how much of the collected material actually belonged to the whale. The researchers found that, on average, approximately 84 per cent of the DNA in the samples came from the animal itself. The remaining material largely included DNA from microorganisms living in the whale's respiratory tract, along with some residual seawater.The researchers were able to produce low-coverage nuclear genomes, which contain genetic information inherited from both parents, alongside high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, which are passed down through the maternal line. To check whether the results were reliable, the team compared samples collected from the same whales during different encounters, including repeat samples gathered across the two years.They also compared the results with conventional biopsy samples from two of the same individuals. The genetic information obtained from the breath samples was consistent with these comparisons, demonstrating that the technique could produce reliable genomic data without requiring conventional tissue sampling.The genetic informationCollection of DNA is only the first part of the process; the actual identification of the genomes begins with sequencing the samples. Three previously undescribed mitochondrial DNA control-region haplotypes in the population were discovered. These are associated with genetic differences at three nucleotide positions, with each haplotype observed in an individual whale. This finding also highlights the effectiveness of the sampling method for studying DNA. The team was also able to determine the sex of every sampled whale using only the genetic data available to them.In concluding the study, researchers were able to ascertain that little evidence was found of recent inbreeding among the specific whales that were studied. Although some stretches of identical genetic material were present, these were seen as more likely to reflect distant shared ancestry or historical population changes. The study also adds to what scientists know about the North Pacific humpback whale population. Before this research, only one publicly available whole genome from a North Pacific humpback whale existed.A new way to study whale healthSince the samples also contain microorganisms from the whales' respiratory systems, researchers could potentially use them to investigate the microbes living in their airways and learn more about respiratory health. The study's authors have further suggested that combining genetic information with microbiome and hormone analysis could even provide insight into the whales' health.The researchers also acknowledge that the technique may not work equally well for every marine species, as factors such as body size, behaviour and the amount of time an animal spends at the surface can influence sample collection.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
