articles.title: As ice receded on a Swiss Alpine pass, archaeologists discovered a bronze neck ring estimated to be 4,000 years old; experts say it is the first Early Bronze Age jewellery found at that location
articles.summary: The job of an archeologist is one that requires immense patience to find something worthy of being called a treasure over the years.
articles.body: The job of an archeologist is one that requires immense patience to find something worthy of being called a treasure over the years. The Earth’s geomorphic cycle has buried centuries of evidence of life on this planet, which is why one of the best sources of human history has been digging around the suspected archeological sites. At the Lötschen Pass, archaeologists have been digging through the same stretch of mountain for years, and the ground there keeps giving things back. The discoveries began with Roman coins and medieval-age arrows.The epochs of the planet have buried secrets of our evolution into the layers of mud, rock, water and ice. Therefore, materials are not just buried under rugged rocks and mud, but in all kinds of landscapes such as underwater and under huge snow-covered glaciers. This is best seen at the Lötschen Pass, more than 2,600 metres above sea level, where since 2011, melting ice has revealed artefacts from the Bronze Age, including bow, arrows, pieces of leather and a box made of wood chips.Meanwhile, graves at Gwatt, Einigen and Hilterfingen have yielded neck jewellery from the same era, worn by men and women. In mid-October 2026, a team from the Archaeological Service of the Canton of Bern found one more piece for this record: a bronze neck ring about 4,000 years old, making it the first Early Bronze Age jewellery ever recorded on the pass.A valuable walkStaff from the Archaeological Service, known as the ADB, regularly walk high-altitude sites to check for prehistoric objects, and the ring turned up on one of those inspection rounds. According to the canton, it is the first larger metal object from prehistory found on the pass.The ring dates to the Early Bronze Age, between 2000 and 1700 BCE. It measures about 13 centimetres in diameter and ends in two small loops shaped like eyelets. The metal is thin, yet after thousands of years in nature, the piece is in surprisingly good shape.The team measured where it lay, documented it and lifted it out with care. It was then taken to the ADB laboratories in Bern, where conservators are treating it now. The Directorate of Education and Culture of the Canton of Bern announced the discovery on Wednesday, 18 November.Why this ring is a firstThe Lötschen Pass sits on the border between the Bernese Oberland and the canton of Valais, and archaeologists have worked there for some time. Since 2011, the melting ice has also given up a Bronze Age bow, arrows, pieces of leather and a box made of wood chips. These organic objects stayed preserved in the ice for centuries, and warming temperatures have exposed them.However, the neck ring is a special discovery for three reasons. First, it lay away from places where the earlier finds have been made. Second, it is the first bronze object recorded on the pass. And lastly, it is the first piece of Early Bronze Age jewellery found there.Mobility through the Alpine passesNeck jewellery like this has turned up before, though in graves rather than on a mountainside. Similar pieces come from the burials of men and women from the same period at Gwatt, Einigen and Hilterfingen, all in the canton of Bern. Sites from the era also exist south of the Bernese Alps in Valais.The Canton of Bern has concluded the Lötschen ring as evidence that people in prehistory moved over long distances, and that Alpine passes have been walked for thousands of years. The pass connects the two regions where these related finds were made.A lost treasure or an intentional oneThe researchers do not think the ring was lost. They suspect someone placed it on the pass on purpose. The canton lists three possible reasons: an offering to a deity, a request for a successful journey, or thanks for one that ended well. Nobody can say which it was, and the announcement does not claim to know.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: More than 8,000 people applied to be NASA astronauts last time and just 10 were picked; applications for the next class are open until 3 December, and most applicants need a STEM master’s and three years’ experience
articles.summary: As children, when science classes first opened us up to the universe beyond our own world, many of us picked up dreams of travelling far and beyond.
articles.body: As children, when science classes first opened us up to the universe beyond our own world, many of us picked up dreams of travelling far and beyond. The white and silver astronaut suits were fascinating, and the idea of exploring a gravity-defying world of space seemed exciting. Leaving the Earth behind, floating around in space and looking at our planet from hundreds of kilometres above sounds like quite an experience, doesn't it? But NASA is actually looking for people to do just that, and if you think getting there is as simple as having a fascination with space, well, there is quite a bit more to it.NASA, the United States' space agency, is now in search of its next group of astronauts, and applications are now open. However, before anyone starts imagining themselves floating around in a spacecraft, there is quite a long list of requirements to get through. The competition is particularly tough, too. As during the previous recruitment round, more than 8,000 people applied, but only 10 were selected.According to NASA's November 7, 2026 announcement, the next group of astronaut candidates will be trained for missions that could take humans back to the Moon, support a permanent human presence on the lunar surface and help lay the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. However, there is a catch. Applicants must be U.S. citizens and hold a master's degree in a STEM field, including engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics, from an accredited institution.A postgraduate qualification, however, is only one part of the requirement. Applicants must also have at least three years of relevant professional experience after completing their qualifying degree. They must be able to pass NASA's long-duration flight astronaut physical, which assesses whether they can meet the physical demands of spaceflight.There are, however, a few alternative routes for those who do not have a conventional STEM master's degree. According to NASA's astronaut eligibility guidelines, two years of work towards a doctoral programme in a relevant technical or scientific field can meet the educational requirement. Certain professional medical qualifications, including a Doctor of Medicine, Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine, Physician Assistant, Doctor of Nursing Practice and Family Nurse Practitioner qualifications, are also accepted. Completing a nationally recognised test pilot school programme is another route, provided the stated conditions are met. If this is the applicant's only advanced technical qualification, a bachelor's degree in a STEM field is also required.The experience requirement also works a little differently for pilots and medical professionals. Pilots can qualify through specific flight-hour requirements instead of the usual three years of professional experience. Depending on the type of aircraft, this can mean 750 hours as pilot in command of a high-performance jet, 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with additional requirements for time spent as pilot in command. For medical doctors, residency training can count towards the experience requirement, provided it is completed by July 2027.Leadership, teamwork and communication skills are only a few of the skills and qualities that the agency is looking for. Once applications are reviewed, a small group of highly qualified candidates may be invited for interviews at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Some are then called back for a second round of interviews, after which the final candidates are selected.The process is followed by another demanding stage. Those chosen do not immediately head into space. They first become astronaut candidates and undergo nearly two years of training at the Johnson Space Center. Over this training period, they learn skills such as spacewalking, operating spacecraft and the International Space Station, flying T-38 jets and controlling robotic arms.NASA's recruitment drive has come at a time when it is working towards some rather ambitious programmes, such as the Artemis project. This programme is focused on returning astronauts to the Moon and creating a more sustained human presence.According to Space.com, in its November 9, 2026 report, NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its astronaut corps. The agency has selected 370 people as astronaut candidates since its first group of seven astronauts was announced in 1959. However, with new spacecraft, spacesuits and missions being developed, the agency is looking to expand the number of people who can take on these responsibilities.NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, who belongs to the 2021 astronaut class, told Space.com that the agency needs more people as it works towards its plans for the Moon, a permanent lunar base and eventually Mars.For those who meet the eligibility requirements, the application window remains open until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Thursday, December 3, 2026. NASA expects to announce its final selections in late 2027, with the new candidates expected to begin their training in winter 2027/2028.The prospect of travelling beyond Earth might still sound like something reserved for a very small group of people. And looking at the numbers from the previous recruitment round, it certainly is a competitive journey. But for someone who's tenacious enough to look up and look high, their dream of working at NASA may be within reach after all.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Lorri Cramer, known as the Turtle Lady of Manhattan, is New York City's only wildlife rehabilitator who works only with turtles, nursing about 36 at a time in her apartment, and one summer she took in 680 babies
articles.summary: Most New Yorkers probably spend their days navigating crowded pavements, squeezing into packed subway carriages and trying to find a little space in an
articles.body: Most New Yorkers probably spend their days navigating crowded pavements, squeezing into packed subway carriages and trying to find a little space in an apartment that is already too small. Lorri Cramer, however, has a rather different problem. Her Manhattan home has to make room for turtles, lots of turtles.Known as the Turtle Lady of Manhattan, Lorri Cramer is a wildlife rehabilitator who has spent decades nursing sick, injured and abandoned turtles back to health from her apartment on the Upper West Side. Her living room has, at various points, looked more like an aquarium than a place to entertain guests, with tanks and plastic tubs occupying the spaces around her furniture. Even the bathroom has had to pull its weight. And while most people might hesitate before bringing home one rescued animal, Cramer once found herself looking after more than 600 baby turtles at once.It is an unusual arrangement, to say the least. But when New York's turtles need help, Cramer is often one of the first people authorities call.An unexpected life with turtlesCramer's relationship with turtles began long before she became the city's unofficial turtle rescue hotline. Growing up in Queens and on Long Island, she spent summers on a boat with her father and grandfather, where she became fascinated by the diamondback terrapins living around Jamaica Bay. She eventually became an art teacher, but her interest in turtles never quite went away.Her rehabilitation work began with the pet turtles belonging to her children. One of her earliest rescues was a North American box turtle named Lavinia, who had been injured after two boys used him as a ball, throwing him back and forth. The turtle arrived with broken legs and a cracked shell. When Cramer took him to an animal hospital, she discovered that nobody there knew how to treat turtles.It was a rather telling introduction to the problem she would spend the next several decades trying to solve. There were plenty of people who could help dogs and cats, but very few who knew what to do with an injured turtle.Cramer eventually became a state-licensed wildlife rehabilitator and the director of turtle rehabilitation at the New York Turtle and Tortoise Society. Her apartment became a place where turtles seized by authorities, abandoned by owners or found injured in the city could receive care. Some arrive after being smuggled into the country, while others are dumped in parks once their owners realise that the tiny pet they bought has grown into a rather less manageable adult.The turtles are not always found in particularly good shape. Some are injured during transport, including those hidden in suitcases or shipped in the cargo holds of aeroplanes. Others are released into unsuitable environments, where they struggle to survive.And then there are the unexpected deliveries.When hundreds of baby turtles arrivedIn 2015 as New York Times reports, Cramer received a call from New York State environmental officials after they seized a shipment of red-eared slider hatchlings from a warehouse in Chinatown. She expected around 50 turtles. Instead, more than 600 arrived at her apartment.The tiny reptiles had to be housed in plastic containers, with Cramer and other volunteers working through the rather enormous task of checking their health and arranging care. Her bathroom became a temporary turtle nursery, with tubs and bins taking over the space.Red-eared sliders are freshwater turtles native to the southern United States and northern Mexico. They are also popular pets, often bought when they are small enough to fit comfortably in someone's palm. The trouble begins when they grow. Owners who are unprepared for their size, needs and long lifespans sometimes abandon them in local ponds and parks.That is not just a problem for the individual animal. Releasing non-native turtles into unfamiliar ecosystems can put pressure on native wildlife, introduce disease and create competition for food and habitat. A turtle that has spent its life in captivity may also have little chance of surviving in the place where it is abandoned.Cramer has seen the consequences first-hand. Turtles have turned up in saltwater, in fountains and in ponds that are entirely unsuitable for their species. Freshwater turtles, for instance, cannot simply be released into the ocean and expected to manage.She has also worked with the New York Turtle and Tortoise Society to address another source of the problem: the practice of releasing captive animals as part of Buddhist fangsheng, or life-release ceremonies. The intention is to save animals and bring good karma, but releasing non-native turtles into the wrong environment can do more harm than good.Rather than dismissing the practice, Cramer worked with Buddhist leaders and wildlife rehabilitators to develop a more responsible alternative. Under the Compassionate Release Life programme, animals that have already been rescued and rehabilitated are blessed before being released into appropriate habitats. It allows the ceremony to continue while giving the animals a much better chance of survival.A home that makes room for everyoneOf course, rehabilitating turtles in a Manhattan apartment comes with its own logistical challenges. There are tanks to clean, food to prepare, injuries to treat and, occasionally, hundreds of hatchlings to find homes for. Cramer has described turning her living room into a makeshift treatment area, with volunteers working in a line to administer eye drops, injections and other care.Her family has had to adjust, too. Her husband, Mitch, reportedly drew the line at having turtles in the bedroom, although he has been willing to buy their food. One of the apartment's bathtubs has also been reserved for human use, while the other has found itself occupied by turtles.Not every animal can be returned to the wild. Some have injuries that make survival outside captivity unlikely, while others are non-native species that cannot safely be released into local habitats. In those cases, Cramer helps arrange adoption or finds suitable organisations to take them in.The New York Turtle and Tortoise Society says she has cared for thousands of turtles over more than 30 years. It is a remarkable amount of work for one person, particularly when the rescue centre is also her home.There is something quietly lovely about the fact that Cramer's work happens in an ordinary city apartment, tucked among the furniture, family life and everyday routines of Manhattan. She did not set out to become the person New York calls when a shipment of baby turtles is discovered or an abandoned tortoise needs help. She simply found that very few people knew how to care for them, and decided someone had to.And so, while the rest of the city gets busy with their own business, Cramer's apartment continues to make room for a few more unexpected residents. Some arrive in need of a little medical attention, others need somewhere safe to grow, and all of them get something they might not otherwise have had: a chance to make it back into the world.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Three dinosaurs found together in 150-million-year-old Wyoming rocks are heading to a Pittsburgh museum; billionaire Ken Griffin's $5 million gift will help build a fossil laboratory where visitors can watch the work
articles.summary: In a rock about 150 million years old in Wyoming, an adult sauropod and two juveniles lay together.
articles.body: In a rock about 150 million years old in Wyoming, an adult sauropod and two juveniles lay together. Between 2023 and 2025, their bones were excavated, and the three were later nicknamed Daisy, Lucky and Lucy. In November 2026, the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh announced that all three are coming to the city on long loans from Ken Griffin, the founder and CEO of Citadel.The fossils are carefully preserved before being on display in a museum. But, these three are not arriving as finished pieces. They will be coming in raw excavated form with a lot of work still remaining to be done on them. While this work is done in back rooms in more places, Pittsburgh plans to do it in public. A $5 million gift from Griffin will build a fossil preparation laboratory where visitors can watch the cleaning, preserving and studying of the three dinosaurs. The money will also fund research, including a study of the rare fossilized skin samples that came with the fossils.The announcement came less than two months after Griffin's record $3 billion pledge to Carnegie Mellon University, also in Pittsburgh.Meet Daisy, Lucky and LucyThe three are sauropods, the long-necked, plant-eating giants. Daisy is an adult, and Lucky and Lucy are juveniles. While their nicknames make them seem like citizens of today, they were actually excavated from rocks about 150 million years old in Wyoming. As reported by the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, the three fossils were found between 2023 and 2025 by the commercial paleontology lab Fossilogic in Washakie County, Wyoming.The lab is the main focusIn most instances, fossil work happens behind the scenes. Pittsburgh's plan is to bring the preparation lab out into the open, where visitors can watch it. A $5 million gift from Griffin will pay for a new fossil preparation laboratory visible to the public. Visitors will be able to watch the uncovering, preserving and studying of Daisy, Lucky and Lucy as it happens.The gift will also fund research on the fossils. One target is the fossilized skin samples that came with the dinosaurs, which are rare. Scientists hope the skin will help them understand these animals better.Carnegie Museum of Natural History Director Dr. Carey Scheide Miller said to CBS News the partnership lets the museum bring the public "directly into the practice of science." She described visitors seeing fossil preparation, conservation, research and discovery as the work happens.How fossil work is usually doneFossil work starts in the field, where a team digs out the bones from the surrounding rock. Because the bones are fragile, the diggers often wrap them in protective coverings before moving them. The bones then travel to a lab, and that is where the slow part begins. This lab would be on display in the Carnegie Museum.Then, technicians remove the leftover rock from each bone, usually with small hand tools, working a little at a time so the fossil is not damaged. Cracked or loose pieces are glued and held together so they don't break further. Each bone is then cleaned, recorded and studied by scientists, who measure it and compare it with other finds. Work like this can take a long time for a single bone, and the three Wyoming sauropods, excavated between 2023 and 2025, still have a lot of it ahead of them.The donor behind the giftGriffin is the founder and CEO of Citadel. The dinosaur news came shortly after another large gift in Pittsburgh. Carnegie Mellon University recently received a $3 billion donation from him, mostly to help build a new campus in Miami, Florida. CBS describes it as the largest gift by an individual in the history of higher education.In his statement, Griffin said Daisy, Lucky and Lucy offer a window into the planet's history. He said he hopes the experiences at the museum will spark curiosity and inspire the next generation of scientists.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Harvard scientist may never prove mysterious space object’s origin after mission scrapped
articles.summary: Avi Loeb claims JAXA's canceled Hayabusa2 landing mission on 1998 KY26 ends the only chance to prove the object is the lost Soviet probe Phobos 1.
articles.body: A Harvard astrophysicist who claims a mysterious object speeding through our solar system is actually a lost Soviet spacecraft says scientists may never be able to get a clear look at it after Japan abruptly scrapped a planned mission to land on the target. Avi Loeb told Fox News Digital that the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's decision to cancel its 2031 Hayabusa2 rendezvous with the object known as 1998 KY26 removes the only opportunity to capture high-resolution images of its surface and settle whether it is a natural space rock or the missing 1988 Soviet probe Phobos 1. "There is no way by which we can actually resolve the object, or get a high-resolution image of its surface, without coming close to it — without a flyby — because even with the Webb telescope or the biggest telescopes we have on Earth, the object is not close enough to be resolved into multiple pixels in an image," Loeb said. MYSTERIOUS OBJECT MOVING THROUGH SPACE COULD BE LOST SOVIET PROBE AS NASA WEIGHS IN ON THEORY The cancellation came just days after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman dismissed speculation about the roughly 36-foot-wide object during an appearance on "Fox & Friends," saying, "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is ... anything other than an asteroid." Loeb pushed back on that assessment, arguing KY26 is "not an asteroid" because it accelerates in a way gravity alone cannot explain and predicting that when Japan's spacecraft lands on it in July 2031, scientists would find a label reading "Made in the USSR" instead of ice or rock. NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS' Japan's space agency reported to the Cabinet Office's Space Policy Committee on Nov. 16 that it was abandoning the 2031 rendezvous after the last normally functioning main ion engine on Hayabusa2 malfunctioned in mid-August, according to the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun. "I was surprised that the cancellation by JAXA occurred just a day or two after I spoke about it publicly, because the malfunction in the engine was known for several months," Loeb said. "The probability that we're dealing with a coincidence where within a day after my public discourse, JAXA decides to cancel this mission is a day divided by the duration over which it was known that the fourth engine is malfunctioning – and that was over 100 days or so. TRUMP HIGHLIGHTS NASA NUCLEAR-POWERED MARS SPACECRAFT MISSION PLANNED FOR 2028 "So, I would argue that the probability for a chance coincidence is less than 1%, but it could still be a coincidence," he added. Loeb noted that Hayabusa2 was designed over several years and questioned why Japanese engineers did not attempt an Earth gravity-assist maneuver to compensate for the lost engine thrust rather than pivoting to another target. JAXA officials said in their report that reaching KY26 in 2031 already required an Earth gravity assist, and that combining working parts from two damaged engines left the 12-year-old spacecraft without enough thrust to perform the necessary orbital changes, prompting a redirect to a 2028 flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510 instead, the newspaper added. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Even without a close-up flyby, Loeb said astronomers still have one major tool left to test his theory from afar by using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to measure the heat radiating off KY26 and analyze its chemical spectrum. SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO "So far, we detected a reflection of sunlight from this object, but the Webb telescope can potentially detect the heat emitted by the object, and that will offer us an opportunity to learn both about the size, the surface temperature of the object, as well as the composition of the object," Loeb said. While mainstream scientists have suggested KY26 is an ordinary rock or comet, Loeb noted the object rotates about once every five minutes and is far brighter than expected. SEND US A TIP Loeb and his colleagues, however, found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of Phobos 1 – a Soviet spacecraft launched toward Mars in July 1988 that shut down after a faulty command – and calculated that sunlight reflecting off its solar panels could produce the observed push without any signs of a "dark comet" tail. GOT A TIP? "It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. articles.title: Historic gold dredging damaged a California river used by salmon and steelhead; a newly approved $3.39 million project aims to restore 20 acres of spawning habitat and reconnect floodplain channels
articles.summary: Conservation efforts have to be carefully chosen based on the geography and its history.
articles.body: Conservation efforts have to be carefully chosen based on the geography and its history. The salmon habitat on the Tuolumne River disappeared years ago when the plains were dug through for the precious gold. A century later restoration efforts for 20 acres of this floodplain have been provided with a $3.39 million grant.In the 1900s, Chinook salmon and Central Valley steelhead used to lay their eggs at the Tuolumne River which lies just downstream from the town of La Grange, in Stanislaus County. In the early 1900s, the machines were put to dig through the riverbed and floodplain here. When the gold ran out, the ecosystem did not automatically recover, it was just bare ridges of rock with barely any soil left. The environment did not remain suitable for the salmon and steelhead to spawn. The Yosemite Rivers Alliance, the Sonora-based nonprofit working on the river, put it plainly: almost none of it works for fish.On November 19, the state's Wildlife Conservation Board (WCB) approved $99.7 million for 24 projects in 17 counties. One of them is a $3.39 million grant to the Yosemite Rivers Alliance for 20 acres of habitat at La Grange.Under the project, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife along with the Yosemite Rivers Alliance will carve out four acres of new side channels and reconnect another sixteen acres of historic floodplain to the river. Crews will also spread fresh spawning gravel along the riverbed and place logs and boulders in the water, giving young fish spots to hide and rest. Native plants will go in along the banks to hold the new ground in place.This is the second and final part of Phase 2, following restoration work of WCB that was funded in February 2026.What "reconnecting" means for a baby salmonThe project will focus on lowering the riverbanks and rebuilding them with porous material that wetland plants can take root in. Thereafter, when the river rises, water will spread across those banks, and baby salmon can swim up onto them.Once there, the young fish feed on small insects and find cover from predators. Non-native bass are common in the river and readily prey on small salmon in open water, so a shallow, planted floodplain gives the baby fishes a safer place to grow larger and stronger before they move downstream. In this way, the restored banks and side channels bring back the kind of nursery habitat that was removed historically.Not the first effortsThe project is not starting from scratch, a part of the project is already finished. On Sept. 4, project managers, partners and neighbors watched the river flow into a newly built meander. Five days later, crews finished a berm across the old main channel, and the river now runs entirely through the new bend. That adds about a quarter-mile of river channel at La Grange. The fish were due back in October.The old landscape had an odd history of its own. An aerial photo the nonprofit shared, estimated at 60 to 75 years old, shows mining tailings piled along the banks and the river shoved north into a narrow path. Those tailings were later scraped up and hauled off as material for New Don Pedro Dam, which left the banks barren and armored with cobble.The funding and the organisations involvedSince 2020, about $8.5 million has gone into planning, designing, permitting and building the first two phases of the La Grange Salmon Habitat Restoration Project. About 85% of that came from two state grants, one from the Department of Water Resources and one from WCB. The rest came from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Department of Fish and Wildlife's Office of Spill Prevention and Response, the Bonneville Environmental Foundation and nonprofit members.There are various organisations involved in the project. They include the engineering firms FlowWest and Applied River Sciences, Triangle Land Restoration, the Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California, Stanislaus Fly Fishers, the Merced-Tuolumne Salmon Alliance, the Upper Merced Watershed Council, Stanislaus County Parks and Recreation, and several landowners who gave up ground to make room for the river.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
